utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. When we closed yesterday, we were hearing submissions from Mr. O'Sullivan, and these will now continue. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good morning. I realize I have 45 minutes left for my submissions, but Mr. Fila has been gracious enough to give me some latitude there, and I'll do my best to finish in the time allotted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've so far found the oral submissions of parties very helpful, and we do not think you should have too close an eye on the clock if you have some helpful information or submission to make to us. And we appreciate there will be the possibility of rebuttal or rejoinder submissions also. And if there are significant points that you feel can be made in that context following what you've heard in court, then it would be helpful to us to hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that. As I said at the outset, my intention is to respond to the submissions of the Prosecutor, both written and oral, and that's the way I intend to continue this morning. At the end of the session yesterday, Judge Chowhan raised two matters and asked me to consider them and respond to them. With your leave, I will deal with one of those points later, and that is the allegation made at paragraph 613 of the Prosecutor's brief that Mr. Milutinovic failed to restrain the VJ by not proposing a session of the Supreme Defence Council and by not proposing an agenda for the Supreme Defence Council. I would straight away like to deal with the other issue raised by the learned Judge, and you asked me, Your Honour, about consultations in relation to appointments in the VJ and the powers of the Supreme Defence Council. My response is this: The Supreme Defence Council does not have the power to appoint; that's Article 136 of the FRY constitution. It is clear that's an exclusive power conferred upon the president of the FRY. Now, the question you asked me yesterday seemed to imply that the Supreme Defence Council did have such a power; we say it does not under the constitution or the Law on the VJ. If it may of assistance, we can refer you to our final written brief paragraph 67 and 70 through 77. The position is this: The president of the FRY is not required to put personnel matters on the agenda of the Supreme Defence Council. He is not required to consult members of the Supreme Defence Council on personnel matters. It's within his discretion to do so. And when he did, when the president of the FRY did put those matters on the agenda, we saw yesterday that information is provided to the members who expressed views and opinions on changes; and in that sense, the members of the Supreme Defence Council are consulted. Now, there are many examples in the record where the president of the FRY did make appointments in the VJ in the relevant period, where there was absolutely no consultation with the Supreme Defence Council because it's his power and his right to do so. And I can give you the examples of General Obradovic who was appointed by President Milosevic as second commander of the -- as commander of the 2nd Army in Montenegro at the end of March 1999. There's the example of Geza Farkas who was appointed by President Milosevic as the chief of the security administration on the 24th of March, 1999. Prosecution witness General Vasiljevic, again appointed by President Milosevic as the assistant to Farkas on the 27th of April. It -- also, I would invite the Chamber to peruse Exhibit P1018. It's a collection of presidential decrees, President Milosevic's decrees, on promotions and decorations in the VJ for the years 1999 and 2000. It's voluminous, it's 350 pages. But we know that during this period, of course, the VSO, Supreme Defence Council, was not meeting. So, in answer to your question, Your Honour, that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to another aspect of the Supreme Defence Council, and it's the allegation made by the Prosecution in relation to the Supreme Defence Council and the Supreme Command. Your Honour, Mr. Milutinovic was not a member of a body called the Supreme Command. The VSO did not become the Supreme Command or become a part of the body called the Supreme Command. The Trial Chamber's had the benefit of all -- of seeing all relevant documentation in relation to the Supreme Command and the Supreme Defence Council. You've seen the laws, the constitution, the minutes of meetings. You've heard the evidence of VJ officers who were members of the body called the Supreme Command, who were present in the underground bunker in Belgrade for 78 days, who were present at daily briefings at the collegium. In our brief at paragraphs 62 to 116, we present the position, and the evidence is this: The body called the Supreme Command was composed of the president of the FRY, supreme commander. And he had a command staff which was the staff of the Supreme Command; in peacetime, this was the General Staff. The president of the FRY was the only civilian in the Supreme Command; and under the principle of military doctrine, of singleness of command, each commander has his staff which implements his orders. What of the evidence? Well, let's begin again with P604, the interview of Mr. Milutinovic with the Prosecutor in 2001. Mr. Milutinovic told the Prosecutor that with the declaration of a state of war by the federal government, everything moved up to the federal level. He told them that the president of the FRY commanded the army through the staff of the Supreme Command, the president of the FRY issued his orders through the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. He told the Prosecutor that the presidents of Montenegro and the president of Serbia had no authority and no role to play in the defence of the country during a state of war. What did the direct participants who testified in this court tell you? There's Prosecution witness General Vasiljevic; Defence witnesses Gajic, Simic, Smiljanic, Curcin, Krga; Court witness Dimitrijevic. All of them said the same thing. All of them confirmed exactly our position, the position that Mr. Milutinovic explained to the Prosecutor in 2001. Indeed, it was the Trial Chamber that explored this issue with the witness Gajic. You asked him what was the composition of the Supreme Defence Council? And you asked him twice -- excuse me, the composition of the Supreme Command. And the Chamber asked him twice on the first day of his testimony and on the fifth day of his testimony. You wanted to know if he was consistent and you wanted to know if he was credible, and he was both. He described the Supreme Command to you. He told you that Mr. Milutinovic was not a member of the Supreme Command, he was not present, he was not involved. He told you that the supreme commander was the only civilian in the Supreme Command. He told you that the Supreme Defence Council had no role and did not meet. Now, in the face of this overwhelming evidence, the Prosecution refers to two witnesses, one of them is Colonel Mucibabic who was a member of the operations administration. He was not a member of the collegium, and he did not attend the collegium. He and Colonel Paskas were responsible for setting up the room for evening briefings, and they took notes. He offered a personal opinion of what he thought the situation was. With all due respect to Colonel Mucibabic, he wasn't in a position to know, and you should disregard what he said in light of all the evidence from the senior officers who were there. The same is true for the second witness the Prosecution cites in their brief, and that's General Obradovic. We deal with him and his evidence at paragraph 101 of our final brief. The Prosecution asked General Simic during his testimony about the testimony of General Obradovic. General Simic said that at the end of March 1999, Obradovic went to Montenegro, where he was the commander of the 2nd Army. General Obradovic was not a member of the staff of the Supreme Command. He was not there, and it was Simic who told you that the members -- who the membership of the Supreme Command Staff was. He said directly that the Supreme Defence Council did not become the Supreme Command, and this was based on the doctrine of singleness of command. He also said the Supreme Defence Council did not meet. Now, what is the evidence of the fact the Supreme Defence Council did not meet? Again, P604, the interview with Mr. Milutinovic; the evidence of these senior VJ officers; the evidence of Mr. Kojic, who was a staff member at Mr. Milutinovic's office, all of which corroborates the submission of Serbia and Montenegro under Rule 54 bis that said there were no meetings of the Supreme Defence Council between the 23rd of March, 1999, and the 5th of October, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was its status during that period, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council existed; it's in their constitution under 135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the state of war doesn't affect the fact that there is a body known as the Supreme Defence Council which can function if the members thereof wish it to function?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: But we say that the Supreme Defence Council had no reason to meet during the state of war. There were competent federal and republic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you leave that point, if a member of the Supreme Defence Council was unhappy on the question whether the supreme commander was commanding the army in accordance with the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, there would be no reason in theory why that member could not seek to have a meeting in view of the new rules that were introduced?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, we say that the Supreme Defence Council did not meet, and it had no reason to meet. With the declaration of war, the competent federal and republic bodies and institutions were functioning and dealing with the question of war and peace and the defence of the country when it was attacked. The Supreme Defence Council, Mr. Milutinovic in particular, had no role, authority, or competence on decisions or determinations in relation to the VJ, the MUP, or other formations engaged in the war effort. The Supreme Defence Council and Mr. Milutinovic would have no role in deliberations or considerations concerning the imminent threat of war, the state of war, or the cessation of war. We know that the VJ is a federal army, and under the constitution is obliged to defend the sovereignty of the country, the independence of the country, and constitutional order. It's commanded solely and exclusively by the federal president. The organs of the federal government, in particular the Ministry of Defence, formulate policy and implement matters of defence and security. We know that the MUP is under the authority of the minister of the interior, who's responsible to the government and ultimately the National Assembly. And we ask you to consider Exhibit 3D670, which is the subordination order of the 18th of April, 1999. We've reproduced that in full in our brief, and I'll review it very briefly here. We say that the subordination order goes to the heart of the matter. It's the only written order issued by the supreme commander during the war, issued by President Milosevic; and it goes to the heart of the matter as I say. We draw your attention to the preamble of the order. The preamble states that the order's issued on the basis of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia and the Law on Defence and the conclusions of the Supreme Defence Council of October 1998. What does this tell us? As we say, it shows that the president of the FRY is the supreme commander and the only competent federal organ in command, that he's empowered under the constitution and the law to make decisions and issue operative orders. Our position is that the Supreme Defence Council is not a command body, it does not plan, and it does not order. And how do we know that? Well, let's look at the reference to the conclusions of the Supreme Defence Council in October 1998, which are referred to in this order of April 19th -- April 18th, 1999. Those minutes are P1575, it's the 6th Session of the Supreme Defence Council on the 4th of October. And there we see that at the conclusion of this rather lengthy discussion, at this point, of course, we have the Security Council resolution of the 23rd of September. The members are discussing how to fulfil their obligations, the call that the UN Security Council has made to Yugoslavia to find a peaceful resolution to the problem in Kosovo. And we see this in the record, and I'll quote: "While bringing the discussion to an end, the president of the FRY and the Supreme Defence Council, Slobodan Milosevic, suggested that the conclusion of this session that would be published in the information be expressed in one -- in only one sentence. Yugoslavia is firm in their choice of peace and ready to resolve all outstanding issues in a peaceful manner; but if we should be attacked, we will defend our country by all means." He put this standpoint as he called it on the table, and it was accepted by both President Milutinovic and President Djukanovic as the standpoint on the issue. We also should look and the Chamber also should look, we say, at P1577, which is the 9th Session of the Supreme Defence Council on the 23rd of March, 1999, on the eve of the war, where President Milosevic reminds the Supreme Defence Council of their standpoint at the session I just mentioned in October and in relation to their position of finding a peaceful resolution and defending if the country's attacked. And this shows, we say, the legal requirements and the involvement of the Supreme Defence Council in relation to state policy concerning the security situation in Kosovo, the threats to its sovereignty, and the need to defend the country if attacked. Now, these political standpoints are adopted unanimously in the form of conditional conclusions, after discussion and consultation among the members of the Supreme Defence Council. The Chamber will also recall that in 1998 at a session of the Supreme Defence Council in June, a similar conclusion was adopted by all members in the conditional, which was: Should terrorist activities of the Albanian separatist movement escalate, the Army of Yugoslavia will intervene in adequate measure. And we know that this conclusion was followed by an operative order of the president of the FRY on the 21st of July, 1998, to fight terrorism in Kosovo which, indeed, had escalated. We also know that the plan for fighting terrorism was prepared, submitted, and approved by the president of the FRY. In the Prosecution's -- I move on now to another matter. In the Prosecution's submissions at pages 26863-26864, he referred to Exhibit 3D728; that's an evening briefing of the 11th of April, 1999. We deal with this matter in our brief at paragraphs 110 to 113. One matter raised by the Prosecutor is the meaning of the abbreviations. We say that "VK" means supreme commander and "VK-DA" means Supreme Command. Now, the evidence on this is clear. We have the evidence of Defence witness Vlajkovic. When he was cross-examined by the Prosecutor at page 16098, he was asked this question: "Q. Before I get to my last question, your last answer was that 'VK' stands for supreme commander; and if you're talking about Supreme Command, then it would be 'VK-DA'? "A. Yes." There was also the evidence of Branko Fezer at page 16487-16488. Now, the Prosecutor also referred to the testimony of Witness Gajic in relation to this evening briefing. Of course, Gajic's testimony is that no politician other than Slobodan Milosevic was a member of the Supreme Command. And Witness Vlajkovic testified that Mr. Milutinovic never attended meetings of the Supreme Command Staff. This evening briefing also lists three other people who testified in this case; that's Exhibit 3D728. Witness Curcin, who testified that General Pavkovic briefed the supreme -- the staff of the Supreme Command in the presence of the supreme commander. And, indeed, in the Prosecution's brief at paragraph 737, they state the same thing, that the briefing was held in the presence of the supreme commander. The other two witnesses who were mentioned in this part of the exhibit are Smiljanic and Krga. They were not asked about 3D728, but we know what their testimony is in relation to the Supreme Command. Smiljanic said the only civilian in the Supreme Command was the supreme commander, Mr. Milosevic. Krga said there was no collective body commanding the VJ. The VJ was commanded by Slobodan Milosevic. In a related matter, the Prosecution referred to Exhibit P1010, a Politika article, a Belgrade daily newspaper; and we say that we can by and large disregard what's in a Belgrade daily on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, it does remain an odd expression. It's understandable in the context that you referred to earlier of General Pavkovic briefing the staff of the Supreme Command, I understand that, and Supreme Command is an appropriate way there of describing the commander. But the more recent reference you've just made, "The only civilian in the Supreme Command was the supreme commander, Mr. Milosevic," that doesn't make much sense to me just as a concept what this Supreme Command is. I understand a commander, I understand the Supreme Command Staff, but I don't understand this: The idea of a body that is the Supreme Command with members that include a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the point is this and the evidence is this, and it was explained by the officers who testified, that every commander has his staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. That's the first way that you've described it; the second way is the way that I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, it's the way that people have expressed it, perhaps. But it's this singleness of command in the army and it's right down the line that it's that way, that the commander has his staff and implements his orders. One person's responsible and one person makes decisions, and we say that's reflected in the subordination order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that would be reflected in peacetime as well. We have this concept of the president commanding the army in peace and war, and he would be the one to issue the orders in peace or in war. So you would have the same concept there. Even when the Supreme Command, as it were, didn't exist, you would still have the supreme commander, the president of the FRY, acting in accordance with the decisions of the opinions of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we quite agree. In fact, President Milosevic is the only person who was able to issue operative orders, but we know that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But in the peacetime context, you have the Supreme Defence Council, so you can understand the various concepts because there is this body that has membership who are not military men. But when we get to the Supreme Command, we have references to membership, but there only is one member effectively in what you're saying and that's where it begins defy common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the membership includes the commander and his staff, and he's the only -- and the difference is that within that command, as opposed to every other command in the army, he is the only civilian who is commander. And during the war, and we talk about this, that is when the term "Supreme Command" is used, and there's historical reasons for that. We point that out in our brief, and that is the mindset, that is the reason that this was used. I mean, we agree that the Law on the VJ didn't change. The fact that the General Staff is now called the staff of the Supreme Command is explained by virtue of the fact of the way that they saw themselves, with President Milosevic commanding through his staff for historical reasons. That was their understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one final point on this, Mr. O'Sullivan, if you can help me personally. Do you remember a witness who rather suggested that the Supreme Command Staff did not necessarily simply turn the command -- the supreme commander's orders into action, and that there was a much greater measure of discretion than we might have thought? A strange answer at the time that seemed to suggest that the staff could act independently of the commander. Now, it may be my mind's playing tricks on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the evidence is this: That -- and I can remember and I know it's General Curcin for sure, and some others, who said that every morning General Ojdanic would meet with President Milosevic and he would then transform President Milosevic's orders into -- in the professional sense and pass them down the line. So it was, again, within the framework of the commander implementing his orders through his staff is entirely the position and the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I now wish to turn to an allegation in the indictment that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Please continue, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I now wish to turn to an allegation in the indictment made by the Prosecution in its submissions, where the indictment alleges that Mr. Milutinovic promoted General Lukic by decree. We say that the correct -- correct position is that the instrument which gave effect to the promotion of General Lukic in May 1999 was an ordinance, not a decree, signed by Mr. Milutinovic. Now, this requires some explanations for a number of reasons, some for linguistic and some are conceptual. Now, the background to this is that in the B/C/S there are two words. The first word is "uredba," u-r-e-d-b-a; and the second word is "ukaz," u-k-a-z. Now, the problem that arose is that CLSS took the position when translating Professor Markovic's expert report, that they translated both of those words from the B/C/S into "decree," which we say is incorrect linguistically and, in particular, in substance, legally. Now, we raised the matter with CLSS; they stood by their guns. We submitted to you court exhibit IC132 which we used during the testimony of Professor Markovic, which clearly made the distinction between "uredba," which is a decree, and "ukaz," which is an ordinance. And I repeat that the position is that the promotion of General Lukic in May was given effect by ordinance, a declarative act signed by President Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you: Are you now going to tell us the difference between a decree and an ordinance?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I shall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Let me first finish the story on the mistranslation, the linguistic problem. In Exhibit 1D680, in the first paragraph, there's a sentence that uses the word "ukaz," and it's been translated by "issue a decree by promoting Sreten Lukic." We say it should say "issue an ordinance promoting Sreten Lukic." Similarly, the cover page of 1D680 in English says "draft decree." It should say "draft ordinance." The second exhibit where there's a problem is 1D722, where again you see the word "decree," where it should be "ordinance" because the B/C/S original is "ukaz." And the last point I want to make before I get to the substance is, again, P604, Mr. Milutinovic's interview with the Prosecutor which was conducted in English and where Mr. Milutinovic used the word "decree." So, in his mind, it wasn't clear either. Now, then, the difference between the concept of decree and ordinance. It's fully discussed and set out in our brief in relation to this matter at paragraphs 55 to 61; it's fully described in the testimony of Professor Markovic. An ordinance is a declarative act; it's similar to the power that the president of the Republic of Serbia has in declaring or promulgating a law. It's a declarative act. It states -- it recognises that a certain fact exists. In some jurisdictions, you may call that royal assent, where you have constitutional monarchies. A decree, on the other hand, is a different document; it's an executive document. And, indeed, as we shall see a little later, the only time that the president of the Republic of Serbia can sign a decree is during the exceptional irregular [Realtime transcript read in error "regular"] state of war; the rest of the time he's only empowered to sign ordinances. It should be "irregular" circumstances. I may have misspoken. The state of war is an irregular circumstance, and I'll come back to that in a different context later. Now, the promotion of General Lukic was an ordinary promotion based on the Law on Ranks, Article 6(1), the promotion is regulated by law. In other words, under Articles 7 and 8 there is objective criteria that if they are fulfilled, then the individual is entitled to a promotion. That's an ordinary promotion. And the ordinance signed by the president really confirms this existing fact: The individual has fulfilled the legal requirements, he's entitled to the promotion. It's a formality. It's a declarative act. The promotion is made in conformity with the law, and the law provided at that time that the ordinance was a required final step in this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just want to learn a bit about the two words, because I thought I understood it earlier but now it's getting a bit rickety. Now, ordinance certainly is a legislative term, and the constitutions provide a life for it and it has to be laid before somebody. It is not something like something permanent. Decree, of course, is an executive order and may not have a life, but appointments usually, as I can think of, should be through a decree. Why through an ordinance? I mean, this is very strange here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I've just consulted my colleague, Mr. Zecevic, and part of the explanation is the words in the Serbian language. The decree, or "uredba," is the executive act linguistically in that language; whereas, "ukaz" is the ordinance, it's declarative. In fact, part of the problem may be the fact that the English language may not capture what the Serbian language or B/C/S language does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That is all right. You are the master of that language and I am learning from you, but you have been telling us through your learned discourse that the appointment was through an ordinance. Now, that means you are using it in the parlance of the ordinance as understood in the English language, so that has been created a bit of confusion. Why would an appointment be made through an ordinance? Why not through a decree? It is, after all, an executive act. This is where things get a bit confused. Thank you very much. I won't bother you further.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We can refer you to the expert opinion of Professor Markovic, and the position is this: That a decree is an instrument issued by an organ with executive power. It comes from the executive body. And an ordinance, or an "ukaz," emanates from a body without executive power. Now, in the context of this promotion, we say it's a promotion according to the law provided for in the law, and the law also said that it required an ordinance, the baptism of the ordinance, to become effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan, with the leave of the Presiding Judge. You have said, though, that the ordinance is of a declarative nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct, correct. It --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Merely declarative.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: That which was necessary has been done before in terms of the appointment, but this is like a formality?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the second point we wish to make in relation to this promotion is that it occurred on the 13th of May, 1999, which is the traditional Security Day in republic. Indeed, Security Day, the 13th of May, had been a traditional police holiday from the days preceding the SFRY and during the SFRY, and including during the life of the FRY. Security Day, as we have shown in our submissions, is a day of, we say, a police holiday, where there are commendations, speeches, public relations, literary contests, awards, memorials. And on the 13th of May, 1999, during the war, of course, the celebration was much more subdued, but on that day Mr. Milutinovic hosted a small reception of some 20 officers from the different branchs of the Ministry of the Interior. You have Exhibit 1D715, which is the draft speech and the list of guests, both of which were prepared in the Ministry of the Interior. It's a purely ceremonial event, a purely ceremonial address Mr. Milutinovic made to the officers that day. He congratulates the MUP on their holiday. He makes an appeal for the bombardment to stop, and for peace and normal life to resume. Now, those are the circumstances surrounding this promotion, a Security Day celebration, an ordinary promotion according to the law. Let me now move to the wartime decrees, which is the only time that the president of the republic may sign decrees. Now, before I get to the substance of that, I will respond to what the Prosecutor said at page 26816, and there he refers to Professor Markovic's expert report, 1D682, paragraph 2.26. Now, Professor Markovic did not say that the decree power is a reserve power under the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. What he did say was that the ability to declare a state of war is a reserve power under the Serbian constitution. In other words, on the issue -- on the matter by virtue of the paramountcy of the federal constitution, the federal organs declare the state of war. And once the state of war is declared, then Article 83(7) of the Serbian constitution becomes operative for the duration of that irregular period, the state of war. And we dealt head on with this matter. We presented the 16 decrees that were presented for signature by the government to Mr. Milutinovic. We also explained, as Article 83(7) provides, that once the state of war ended, there was a requirement to submit those decrees to the National Assembly, which he did. And we deal with that in paragraphs 21 to 54 of our brief. Now, contrary to the allegations of the Prosecution, we say that Mr. Milutinovic did not use the decree power to further a JCE; that's contrary to the law and the facts and completely misconstrued by the Prosecutor. As I just said, the ability to sign the decree under 83(7) is contingent to an irregular situation, a state of war that has been declared by the body. The four decrees are of relevance, we say, and all four decrees are dated the 6th of April, 1999, and I'll explain why those four are important. There's the decree on internal affairs, the decree of assembly of citizens, the decree on domicile and residents, and the decree on ID cards. Now, all four of these decrees were presented to Mr. Milutinovic for signature on the 6th of April. All four of these decrees or similar decrees had already been on the books in the former Yugoslavia in the SFRY. They were standard decrees that would be implemented in the case of a state of war. The decree on internal affairs expanded the ability of a superior in the MUP to impose measures to punish subordinates. It enlarged the list of grave offences, which included the prohibition of the exhibition of national, racial, or religious intolerance. Among other things, I would submit that this shows that there certainly was no way to argue that this was a furtherance of a JCE, when the powers of the superiors to punish subordinates is expanded and there's a grave offence for the exhibition of national, religious, or racial intolerance; in fact, that shows just the contrary. The decree on assembly imposes the restrictions on public assembly, the decree on ID cards lowers the age from 16 to 14, and the decree on resident provides that residents must register their domicile. Now, in relation to all four of these decrees, there is a statement of reason which accompanies it, it accompanies all four of them; and statement of reasons states that it's to create the prerequisite for the Ministry of the Interior to carry out its function efficiently in wartime conditions. We say it's important for the state to know where citizens are living, to be able to identify its citizens in case of mobilisation or casualty. Lowering the age from 16 to 14 could deal with questions of delinquency. There's questions of public safety and assembly, rationalised food, and so on. There's nothing criminal or nefarious about any of these decrees, and it's pure fancy to suggest that there is. On the same day when there's a decree -- a proposal from the government, a decision from the government, to make the MUP work more efficiently, it defies logic to say, well, at the same time, they're proposing decrees on residents and ID cards to make sure that they can expel the Albanian citizens. There's no connection between these four decrees and any kind of criminal conduct or intent or anything of the sort. I would like to move now to the final part of my submissions, and in this part I will deal with His Honour's question from yesterday; and it has to do with state of mind, Mr. Milutinovic's state of mind, what animated his conduct. Now, we know that is during the relevant period of 1998 and 1999. Well, in 1998, Mr. Milutinovic knows that there's an armed insurrection happening in part of the territory of the Republic of Serbia, he knows all the steps that are being taken by the republic and federal levels. And, indeed, at the Supreme Defence Council meeting on the 4th of October where the position of seeking peace primarily and defending if attacked, on the 4th of October, Mr. Milutinovic says: "We must do everything. If more needs to be done, we should do it." And, of course, that is the period, October-November, that Mr. Milutinovic is most active in the negotiation of process, of trying to achieve negotiation. At paragraph 630, the Prosecution refers to in its brief, 630, it refers to Exhibit 2827, which is a document from the deputy minister of information on the 1st of October, 1998. It arrives on Mr. Milutinovic's desk, and it refers to media reports in Western media in relation to Gornje Obrinje. Now, the Ministry of Information is reporting that Western media has stated and Albanian press has stated that there's an alleged massacre of Albanian citizens, civilians, by the Serbian police in Gornje Obrinje. And the Ministry of Information says this, and I'm quoting: "Officials of the Ministry of the Interior deny that its members conducted operations against civilians, adding that an investigation would be launched into the alleged crime which they learned about from the Western media. The Ministry of Information denied the reports in the foreign media via the internet and in letters to foreign editorial offices." Now, here the president is receiving information from the Ministry of Information. He's informed that the MUP has denied the accuracy of the foreign media and that an investigation is going to be undertaken. Now, clearly that is a -- Mr. Milutinovic's state of mind there is that he's informed that the proper functioning channels are going to deal with it. I don't think there's any dispute in this case from either side that the MUP and the VJ were sophisticated structures with competent people that functioned during 1998 and 1999. And here the president of the republic is informed that precisely that is going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe that is not very relevant, but I'm confused with respect to the periphery of time. I've read the brief of the Prosecution, where they make a mention of a report sent by a Prosecutor from this place to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, did that activate anybody there or did it come to the notice of your client or something or any action taken, because nothing has been said on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what the Prosecution fails to point out is that the evidence of Mr. Kojic, who was in Mr. Milutinovic's office, was that that letter was never received by his office; whereas, Mr. Kojic did confirm that this exhibit, 2827, was received. I turn now to some of the allegations made by the Prosecution questioning why Mr. Milutinovic should be present at international meetings, and that was at transcript 26815. And Prosecution asked why did Professor Markovic say that Mr. Milutinovic did not conduct foreign relations and relations with foreign organizations. Well, the only reason that was addressed by us is because paragraph 8.1 of the indictment alleges it, and it demonstrates a complete misunderstanding of the constitutions of the FRY and Serbia, because on the basis of paramountcy, foreign relations are strictly within the realm of the federal government. That's why it was addressed. Now, was Mr. Milutinovic present at certain meetings? Yes, he was. Ambassador Vollebaek, head of the OSCE, said he met Mr. Milosevic on one or two occasions, and at one or two of those meetings Mr. Milutinovic was present. And in his evidence, P2634, paragraph 39, Mr. Vollebaek says this in relation to Mr. Milutinovic's presence: "I believe that this was to indicate that Kosovo was a part of Serbia, and they did not want to talk about Kosovo without the president of Serbia present." Well, we know that one of the constitutional provisions of the Republic of Serbia -- Constitution of the Republic of Serbia is that the role of the president is to symbolise unity of the state. Then the Prosecutor asked: "Well, where did Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Milutinovic sit in relation to one another?" And the answer was that Mr. Milutinovic sat to the right of Mr. Milosevic. I believe that's what's called protocol. We've all seen people sitting in circles in big comfortable chairs and sofas, and you have the head of state and to his left was sitting the president of the republic. General Naumann, there's a supplement information sheet, P2561, in relation to the technical negotiations which took place in October on reducing VJ and MUP forces in Kosovo to stabilize Kosovo. The Prosecution for some reason doesn't mention the supplemental information given by General Naumann, which one would think the questions are puts to Mr. Naumann so that he can clarify the position. He said Mr. Milutinovic was present and not very active. Now, why would he be very active? This is a very technical meeting where MUP and VJ people with all the information about forces and logistics are there, and they're negotiating with Clark, Naumann, Byrnes, and the rest. What we do say about this, however, is it goes to Mr. Milutinovic's state of mind. He realizes that they are complying with the UN resolution to withdraw, he knows that his main task at that point is to seek a political solution, he's working with the state delegation, and here he is present when the points of the October Agreements are being hashed out. The Prosecution also refers to a man named Phillips who testified, and Phillips attended the meeting with William Walker and Mr. Milosevic. Now, initially, Phillips claimed that Mr. Milutinovic was present. He was challenged on that. He was asked to give a date; he gave dates. He was shown newspaper articles, and Mr. Milutinovic is not present. Finally, he concedes -- Phillips concedes: "After all this time, I may very well -- I could very well be wrong." We've explained Mr. Milutinovic's presence with meeting Hill and Petritsch in 1998 and being in France in 1999. Turning to paragraph 613 of the Prosecutor's brief, we say it misrepresents the evidence that in 1998 and early 1999, Mr. Milutinovic was preventing and others were preventing the ICTY from investigating in Serbia. Now, we're in 1998 and 1999, and the key things here are to remember that in relation to Racak and in relation to Radonjic lake, there were investigations by local authorities and foreign forensic people, the Finnish were there. It was an internal matter because ICTY jurisdiction applies when there is an armed conflict. There was no armed conflict in 1998 and early 1999. Those were purely domestic matters, and they were being investigated. Nobody can say anything to the contrary. Indeed, the Prosecutor called Dr. Dunjic and his colleague to testify. Perfectly legitimate position taken by the authorities. There's no abdication of responsibility, there were investigations. The OTP brief at paragraph 565. I'll give you the reference and I'll ask you to read it at your leisure because it's not easy to explain orally. There the Prosecution is alleging -- the Prosecution provides a quotation from Mr. Milutinovic's interview with the Prosecutor, P604. It's pages 150 and 151, and they say it shows that Mr. Milutinovic had influence over Mr. Milosevic. Now, I'm going to ask you to look at paragraph 565, and then look at the reference in Mr. Milutinovic's interview, page 150-151, because in the interview, the investigator says -- asks Mr. Milutinovic: "Were you ever very close to Mr. Milosevic?" His answer is: "No, I couldn't say that I was close." Now, that sentence is not included in the brief. So I just ask you to read the full context of the questions and answers, and you'll see that the inference or the submission doesn't follow at all. Bombing will lead to massacres. It's Mr. Milutinovic's position that he categorically denies that he ever uttered those words to Mr. Petritsch or anyone else. We've analysed the evidence in this case at paragraphs 216 to 221. The Prosecution's brief provides no analysis of this because it cannot withstand scrutiny. Mr. Milutinovic never said those words. Ambassador Petritsch told you that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there evidence that he denies it? Just so that there's no misunderstanding here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That's our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it's not in the interview, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Of course, his interview took place, and he was not asked by the Prosecutor about any of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, the evidence is, as you know, that Mr. Petritsch does not recall Mr. Milutinovic ever saying this at a meeting with him. He admits that he's rationalised it eight years after the fact after seeing a memo. He never even mentioned that he spoke to Mr. Milutinovic at Rambouillet when he was interviewed by the Prosecutor in May and June 1999, a few short months after the events. The Prosecutor in its submission says the interview in May took place in very intense circumstances. Well, there was two sessions, one was the 14th of May and the second was the 9th of June. What's intense about that? When Ambassador Petritsch testified in Milosevic, he never mentioned that he ever spoke with Mr. Milutinovic at Rambouillet. Now, the Prosecution says we didn't cross-examine Petritsch on that fact. There's no need to cross-examine him on that fact; it's part of his testimony. We're just pointing out in submission that this is his evidence. The memo in question is P562. If you look at the memo, it does not say that Mr. Milutinovic says, Bombing Serbia will lead to massacres. That's the first point. But we do know that Mr. Petritsch has attributed those words to Mr. Stambuk in his interview at the Milosevic trial, and he comes here and says, well, Stambuk and Milutinovic both said it and exactly the same change. In our brief, we show the parallels, that he asked the same questions of both men, and both men said the same thing in the same context, hardly. We ask you to review that evidence. In the final brief of the Prosecutor, paragraph 45 says, according to Petritsch: "It's very, very unlikely that a mistake was made at the time of the dispatch."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a submission about -- you've been over Petritsch in detail yesterday as well. Do you have a submission about why he would give us inaccurate evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Because he's mistaken, he's rationalised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is the basis on which you say that his evidence is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 216 of our brief, we review the circumstances surrounding the creation of that memo. We know that memos are created ad hoc according to the testimony of Petritsch and Kickert. This particular memo was prepared at 6.00 in the morning on the 20th of February by Kickert, who was not -- never claims to be present at any meeting between Mr. Petritsch and Mr. Mayorski and Mr. Milutinovic. Now, we know that on the night of the 19th and 20th at Rambouillet, Ambassador Petritsch was working with the state delegation from 7.00 p.m. until 5.00 in the morning. That's the evidence of Professor Markovic, that's the evidence of Kickert. He also met in the early morning of the 20th with the Albanian delegation. Remember, the 20th of February is the day when the first ministers of the Contact Group were coming to the castle, when the two parties presented their views and their positions on the political components of the Rambouillet agreement; that's the 20th. So all that night before, from 7.00 p.m. Friday until 5.00 in the morning Saturday, Petritsch is with the delegation and they're working on the agreement. They're working all night, it's charged, it's hectic, it's busy, and common sense tells you that that's a perfect formula for mistakes to happen, mistakes to occur. And Kickert acknowledged that because he pointed out that dispatches were made in that kind of environment, this one and others. And when one other dispatch from 1998 was pointed -- was shown to him and it contained a mistake, he says, "Well, yes, those are the kind of things that can happen; you can get a name wrong." So those are the surrounding circumstances. It's rationalised by Petritsch, he doesn't recall it, never talked about it, and the circumstances surrounding that memo which he say refreshed his memory are unreliable. That's why we say it never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the points you raised about Petritsch yesterday, am I right in thinking your submission went further than simply that he was mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: In regards to the other aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, the negotiations themselves. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, I'm talking at this point about Mr. Milutinovic's state of mind and what he was aware of, what he knew, what he legitimately believed during the war. I'm moving to that now. We can look at that based on the information available to him during the war, the meetings he attended, people who was in contact with. Now, his -- the person from his office, Mr. Kojic, told you that Mr. Milutinovic dealt with civilian matters, removal of hazardous material, food supply, electrical supply. You know that Mr. Milutinovic travelled to Vojvodina, to Novi Sad, which, in fact, is where the NATO bombings began from the first day, where oil refineries were hit and bridges were taken out. Mr. Milutinovic was meeting with the deputy prime minister of Serbia, Mr. Tomic, Mr. Cosic testified, the minister of energy, Mr. Babic, the general manager of the electrical industry. Now, remember, Mr. Milutinovic has already told the Prosecutor that with the declaration of war, the federal organs are conducting the war effort and defending the country. He attends weekly meetings, short meetings, meetings that lasted less than half an hour with the dual purpose of getting a briefing on wartime conditions; by that, we mean protection of the population, economy, diplomatic issues, trying to find a way to end the war, rebuilding the country. And we also know that the second reason for those meetings was to give assurances to the population. Now, there's a history of World War II which was very painful for Serbia when the Nazis bombed the city on the 6th of April, 1941, when the king and the government left the country for Cairo. Very painful memories for that in the country. And part of those meetings was to publicize that the leadership was still in the country. There were people from the federal government and the republic government discussing these matters, but it was also used to broadcast and to publicize on the front page of the daily newspapers. Now, to state the obvious, at none of these meetings is there discussion about committing crimes against the Albanian civilians or the plan to expel or how is it going in succeeding in the plan to expel. Then we look at the information Mr. Milutinovic received. He received information on the destruction of -- caused by the NATO bombing. He received all the reports on the hazardous materials, food, electricity, telecommunications. He received information from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, he received MUP bulletins, he received the intelligent department briefings from the VJ, he received the daily combat reports from the VJ. His staff summarized information they received from the international and domestic media and other sources for him when he arrived in the office, so that he knows what's going on. And we say that based on all this information, Mr. Milutinovic knows and believes that the competent structures authorised to conduct the war during the state of war were fully functioning, fully operational, fulfilling their duties and their obligations. There was no evidence to suggest they weren't. And what else is he aware of? Well, on the 6th of April, he's aware of the unilateral proposal for a cease-fire from both levels of government. He's aware on the 8th of April that the federal government has denounced the heightened NATO bombardment during this period, the very period where the government has asked -- jointly, the governments have asked for a cease-fire for Easter period. He knows the federal government has made an appeal to the world for humanitarian aid. Mr. Bulatovic said that would include aid to the Kosovar Albanians. Mr. Milutinovic knows that in early April, the staff of the Supreme Command made a public announcement condemning NATO and asking for the bombardment to stop and for people to return home. You'll see in our brief that we made a brief selection of the VJ intelligence documents, but we ask you to read them all. On the 3rd of April, the VJ intelligence says that: "NATO is planting information in the Albanian diaspora; but within the next 24 to 48 hours, they'll begin indiscriminate bombing and raze Kosovo and Metohija to the ground." On the 25th of April, the intelligence documents say that the Kosovar Albanian refugees are being sent in circles by the CIA at the Macedonia-Albanian border to generate public support for NATO. And the suggestion of the intelligence document says: "We should call once again on the refugees to return home." On the 12th of May, the intelligence report says that the West is still manipulating the question of refugees. Now, when General Krga was here he testified about this particular document, and he said that every option and initiative to find a peaceful solution to end the war was being sought. They were creating conditions -- trying to create conditions for the cessation of air attacks and to launch dialogue. And he said that one of the factors that the VJ was counting on was the return of refugees [Realtime transcript read in error "VJ"]. He knew of no one and believed that no one had the aim of expelling them. 25th of May, Mr. Milutinovic learns that there are 4.000 -- that 4.000 refugees returned from Macedonia in one day; and the next day, by noon, there were 400 NATO sorties including B-52 and B-18 bombers. And the analysis of this is that it's supporting the KLA breakthrough. The consequence is that previously destroyed targets were hit, and this spread panic and demoralised the population in the region. When you review these documents that crossed his desk, Mr. Milutinovic is told that there's a functioning military court system with prosecutors and that there are complaints and investigations. Now, that's his state of mind, that's the information he has. Mr. Milutinovic knew of no plan, never heard of a plan to expel Albanians, he never intended to harm anyone, he never conducted himself in any fashion whatsoever that could begin to be construed as criminal, and yet the Prosecution claims that there's omission on his part. Well, let's look back at one of the decrees, the decree I mentioned early under 83(7), where the government takes over temporarily from the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Here, at page 33, line 11, I think you meant something else instead of the word "VJ" there, "return of VJ," am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, "the return of refugees."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The VJ was counting on the return of refugees. Thank you. Now, this is the decree on internal affairs. I would like you, the Chamber, to read paragraphs 1079 and 1080 of the Prosecutor's brief. There the Prosecutor's position is that this decree on internal affairs provided MUP officials with greater power to detain suspects, restrict movement, perform searchs, to carry out orders unless ordered to carry out criminal acts, to implement more efficient disciplinary measures. As I mentioned earlier, there was also the grave offence in the exhibition of national, religious, racial intolerance is included. Now, Mr. Milutinovic is aware of this document; he signed the decree. He has every reason to believe that the MUP structures are functioning and their functioning with greater powers than they had in peacetime, in conformity with the law. And in this regard, I would refer the Chamber to -- additionally to paragraphs 34 and 38 of our brief and paragraphs 28 to 33 of our brief. And this might be the appropriate time for me just briefly to make a comment about the submissions made by my learned friends by Mr. Markovic and his expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. O'Sullivan, while we are quite happy to be flexible about the use of time, we also have to have regard to the fairness of the situation and the way in which the Prosecution certainly recognised the terms of the order we made. So I don't think you should regard yourself as having a free hand to repeat again a lot of what's in the brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Then I'll move to the two matters and I'll be finished. The first matter is to deal with Judge Chowhan's question about the VSO. What I've been describing here is Mr. Milutinovic's state of mind, his awareness, the information at hand. He knows the VJ had no plan to expel. The VJ is commenting on manipulation of refugees by the CIA. He knows the wartime courts are functioning. He knows the civilian courts are functioning. These intelligence reports also say that there's manipulation in the Western media, falsehoods in the Western media, which are unfounded. And we've referred to those submissions in our brief chapter and verse on that. So there's absolutely no reason for him to think that anything untoward is happening or that there's any reason to propose a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council. His understanding, of course, on the basis of who's commanding the army, on the army's functioning in the wartime is clear. There's no basis for him, for a man in his position, with his information, with his activities during the war, to think that there's a reason to convene or propose the meeting be convened. That's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I do wish to conclude by referring to evidence regarding Mr. Rugova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that, you should not be diverted from dealing with the criticism of Markovic's expertise. I didn't interrupt to stop you doing that, but just to make sure we focus on what you really need to address and I think that is something you do need to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, very well. We would ask the Court, first, to look at 1D684, that's his curriculum vitae; and we point out that the Prosecution has acknowledged that he's an expert in the field of constitutional law, given his training and expertise. And we called him to deal with the allegations in the indictment which are completely misguided on the constitution and authority and competence of the president of the FRY; that's in part 3 of our brief. And we think it's somewhat disingenuous or very close to being disingenuous for the Prosecution to make submissions when they did not call a constitutional expert. They dropped their first one and would not even disclose to us the report of the second one. I think it's a fair comment to say the reason they didn't call someone is because that expert wouldn't say what they wanted to hear. Now, the fact that Professor Markovic is also in government, also working in the peace process, he's there because of his constitutional expertise. There's nothing in his opinion, interpretation of the constitution, that would suggest bias, we say. I mean, you can make a blanket statement, but there's no detail of that. It certainly doesn't come out of his cross-examination. And, indeed, in some points of the Prosecutor's submissions, they referred to Professor Markovic. So a blanket condemnation of someone without any detail is untenable; and, quite frankly, we've put in annex 1 of our brief a full review of his expertise and his expert testimony. We say it's rock solid, explains the situation, and it shows the frailties and the weaknesses of the Prosecution's submissions or allegations. The evidence of Dr. Rugova -- regarding Dr. Rugova in spring of 1999, the evidence is that the international media had reported at the beginning of the war that Dr. Rugova was killed or wounded. Well, quite untrue. The Prosecution says that the contacts with Dr. Rugova are part of a Serb propaganda campaign. We deal with this at paragraph 261 and 271 to 276 of our brief. For some reason, the Prosecution's insisting that there was house arrest; nothing can be further from the truth. Dr. Rugova met with Mr. Milosevic on the 1st of April, and said he needed to travel abroad to contact his key people. The next day -- prior to that, state security had been ordered to protect him. The next day, they connect CNN television in his house, they connect the phone line in his house. Mr. Merovci is calling Skopje, speaking Chris Hill. Mr. Rugova's associates, Mr. Shala, Mr. Ramoj [phoen], Mr. Kortesi [phoen], are located in Kosovo, and Mr. Rugova is asked: Do you want to meet them? Mr. Merovci said he demanded, the word he used was demanded, that his family is children be allowed to travel to Skopje, and they were at the beginning of April. Between the 17th and the 21st of April, Mr. Merovci himself travelled to Skopje, and travel arrangements were made by state security. There he met Petritsch, Hill, William Walker. Mr. Rugova was giving press statements. He had a press conference with the Russian ambassador. He met with the Russian patriarch Aleksei. He met on the 16th of April in Belgrade with Mr. Milutinovic. Here's the Prosecution evidence on that meeting: Mr. Rugova and Mr. Merovci arrived in Belgrade with police escort. There was a pleasant meeting. Mr. Rugova did not -- there's no complaint about house arrest. Mr. Rugova told Mr. Milutinovic that the majority of his party members or collaborators were in the west. He needed to leave the FRY. He needed to meet and work with party members. Mr. Milutinovic knew of his very difficult situation, that he'd spoken out publicly against the KLA, and Mr. Milutinovic said that Rugova had been pushed out by the KLA at Rambouillet. Mr. Milutinovic said very diplomatically, "Kosovo is yours, you are a person, a leader of the citizens of Kosovo, and the responsibility lies with you." Mr. Milutinovic said this to Rugova in this meeting. Mr. Rugova indicated he wanted to go to Macedonia. Mr. Milutinovic said it wouldn't be safe for him in Macedonia. Mr. Rugova said he wanted to go to Italy. Mr. Milutinovic phoned Foreign Minister Dini, the Italian foreign minister. The Italians accepted, they sent the plane; and Rugova, Merovci, and other family members travelled to Rome. What's the basis of this evidence? P604, Mr. Milutinovic's interview with the Prosecutor where he told them that, and the testimony of Adnan Merovci. Now, the evidence from these two people who were present at the meeting, there's no mention that Dr. Rugova said to Mr. Milutinovic that Kosovo was being emptied by oppression and violence. There's no account that Mr. Milutinovic said that the outcome -- that this was the outcome of the international community. Now, there's a matter of law and fact here which we say is important. The Rugova statement is admitted under Rule 92 quater, because Mr. Rugova, the late Dr. Rugova, obviously could not attend. So there was no ability for us to have confronted Dr. Rugova. We say you can accord no weight to what's in that statement because it's completely uncorroborated. In fact, it's contradicted by what Mr. Milutinovic told the Prosecutor and by what Mr. Merovci told the Prosecutor. There's no mention of Rugova saying there's oppression and emptying Kosovo in the statement of Mr. Merovci. The Prosecution never asked Mr. Merovci if this is correct, but Mr. Milutinovic was interviewed by the Prosecutor. It was the 12th and 13th of November, 2001. Rugova had been interviewed by the Prosecutor on the 1st and 3rd of November, 2001. Prosecutor interviewers never challenged Mr. Milutinovic's evidence. Let me turn to the meeting in Pristina on the 28th, where there is a joint declaration aimed at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Just a word, please. I apologise for interruption. Now, in context with Rugova and those days when then his house was visited by your client and all, now there's also a journalist lady staying with him. What significance does that have, because I think she did utter a few things . And, secondly, when he's being called as the diplomat of Kosovo and all that, he also gives a symbolic gift. What does that indicate? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. The meeting on the 16th was in Belgrade. Mr. Milutinovic never visited his home. The symbolic gift was presented by Dr. Rugova to Mr. Milutinovic in Pristina on the 28th, and we know that that is a sign, a traditional sign of respect, that Dr. Rugova presented crystals to individuals when he met with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: So, culturally, that's something of respect, nothing otherwise, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if it's cultural, it's just something that Dr. Rugova did. Kosovo's rich in minerals, and for him it symbolised Kosovo. And it was a sign of respect and friendship that he presented to people, certain individuals when he met them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But you did take the stand that wherever he was, he was not under house arrest or anything of that sort. That is what you're saying, is it? In that context, I was mentioning about that lady journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it may very well be a state of mind of Dr. Rugova and Mr. Merovci at the time. I'm sure they were scared. They were concerned, they had to be. They didn't know what would happen to them. But eight years later, we have the evidence of the state security man and all the events that surrounded this whole event. The press report saying that -- the Western report saying that he's dead; he's not. He's the only interlocutor, the key interlocutor, that the Serbian side at least have reasonable interlocutor. Now, were they scared? I'm sure they were scared until the plane landed in Rome, but the fact of the matter is they were sent to Rome. Mr. Milutinovic said: "Don't go to Macedonia, it's dangerous for you there." Now who would the danger be if anyone but the KLA in Macedonia. That's, I think, how I would -- we submit that is the proper interpretation of Mr. Milutinovic saying, "Don't go to Macedonia." Then Mr. Milutinovic turns around and says, "All right. I'll phone Mr. Dini, the foreign minister." Now, if there's a plan to ethnically cleanse, don't you get rid of the leadership first? You don't save lives. You don't tell the man, You're the legitimate leader. And for -- the Prosecution says, Well, that Dr. Rugova in the Milosevic trial said they were doing this to discredit him, but they don't look at the next question Mr. Nice asked Mr. Rugova, and say, "Well, were you discredited? He said, "Of course not. I was elected president in 2000 and 2001 of Kosovo." None of this is a sign of anything on the part of Mr. Milutinovic and others to stop the bombing, to stop the madness, including Rugova. Why would he want his people bombed, and to attempt to once again engage in that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's very kind. Thank you. But please tell me when your client gives him that place, now why his role in the peace talks was, as we saw in the evidence, not very prominent, Dr. Rugova's. Why didn't you induct him that way? Why didn't you put him at the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I think the reason Dr. Rugova was not prominent at Rambouillet is because the KLA were in control, Mr. Thaqi and others. Mr. Rugova had been sidelined. As we from that Rule 70 document, he was under pressure from the KLA not to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No. But is there any expression of your desire to have him there or deal with him in those talks because you were, after all, a party.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You're talking about Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: He was a part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: No, no, overall. I'm talking about overall negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, he had been invited numerous times in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What about later than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, this meeting that he and Mr. Milutinovic had on April 28th was again a request to resume -- in 1999, to stop the bombing and resume talks and to have a Temporary Executive Council until a permanent body was -- legislative body could be established in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say on the point of the journalist that was included in that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The point of the journalist fades completely when we look at everything that was done to accommodate Mr. Merovci and Mr. Rugova. Now, the last point I'll make is in relation to the meeting on the 28th in Pristina, and I ask you to look at transcript 8469-8471. Mr. Merovci has been in Dr. Rugova's house since the 31st of March. He returned to his flat twice. He was escorted by the police to his flat twice. His Albanian neighbour is still living in her apartment. Now, she tells him that a policeman had come to his flat with a dog, and obviously it had been damaged and destroyed. As well, it had been ransacked. Now, certainly, that's the full context of the statement Mr. Merovci made to Mr. Milutinovic at that meeting. He said that people were being forced out of their homes, his neighbour wasn't, and that his flat had been destroyed and it had been done by the MUP. And Mr. Milutinovic expressed surprise at that. We say the neighbour's still living in her flat. His house may have been ransacked, yes. We don't know what other information or what other steps were taken by those on the ground in Pristina to find out what happened. We say that certainly isn't evidence that should put Mr. Milutinovic on notice, given the full context that there's some nefarious crimes going on here. To conclude, Your Honour, we have nothing to add to part 5 of our brief where we review charges and the law. We hold the Prosecution to strict proof of all the elements in the indictment. We wish to adopt certain submissions of co-accused, the Ojdanic brief part 4, legal issues and responsibilities; the Pavkovic brief, the legal submissions contained in paragraph 11 to 48 and 340 to 358; we adopt the submissions of the co-accused on crime base and evidence of no plan and no JCE. Finally, two evidentiary points. P2166, a document that purports to be minutes of the inter-departmental staff. We refer you to our brief at paragraphs 176 to 178. We say that it's an unreliable document. We objected the first time it was tendered. The second point is paragraph 4 of the OTP brief, which says that except for the Lazarevic interview, you are not invited to rely on any of the statements of the co-accused to prove the acts or conducts of an accused. Those are our responses to the Prosecution's submission. We say our written brief fully addresses every issue, every allegation, and Mr. Milutinovic was never involved in any conduct at all, never manifested criminal intent. And one last point: He's a man who sought solutions through dialogue and compromise. We know that he had been a politician most of his adult life and a diplomat, and there's no possible connection between, we say, between Mr. Milutinovic and radical politicians or radical speech. And, in fact, in P604, his interview with the Prosecutor, annex 24, he says this about Mr. Seselj, a man he defeated to become president in 1997. Mr. Milutinovic says: "Mr. Seselj had an extreme rightist and fascist approach to all questions in Yugoslavia." The complete antithesis of what Mr. Milutinovic advocated, said, and practiced. I thank you for your attention, Your Honours. Those are our submissions and we request a full acquittal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. We'll adjourn now and resume at 11.15. --- Break taken at 10.49 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we shall now hear your submissions on behalf of Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned friends, I hope we are friends because we've been together long enough, I wish to say to you and to take this opportunity because this is my last address to the Court, and you will address us in due course, to say two things. Firstly, I acted for 12 and a half years before this Tribunal; it's a long time even for me. And now that I'm about to leave, I remembered a wonderful speech made by Napoleon Bonaparte, who addressed his soldiers who participated in the battle of Austerlitz. He said: "Be happy because all your life you will be able to say I took part in it." It has been an honour for me to have taken part here, and I am especially gratified to have taken part in this trial truly because it has been conducted on a highly professional level, both by Your Honours and by my learned friends and the other Defence counsel. I was afraid it might be like the Milosevic trial, and I'm glad that my fears were not confirmed. For all these reasons, I cannot mention any successes in track and field by Serbia as my colleague from Jamaica was able to do, but I can tell you wonderful a French saying, which is "partir, c'est un peu mourir," which means, "every time you say good-bye, you die a little," and that is the feeling I have here now that I'm about to leave you. Let me now move on to the substance of the matter. I will not say anything about my final brief for two reasons: Firstly, because I promised you I wouldn't if you remember correctly in order to avoid bothering both you and myself and the Prosecutor; and, secondly, because I belong to a law school which doesn't consider closing arguments to be worth much because when a Defence counsel is well prepared, when a counsel presents the right evidence, if the trial is concluded and the Judges have no idea what the counsel was trying to prove, you've wasted your money. So I hope that my Defence case became clear in the course of its presentation, and I don't know what I should add. So I will deal only with the closing arguments of the Prosecutor which we have heard here in the past two days. And, unfortunately, I have to abide by what I said before, that the level of evidence presented by the Prosecution - and I said this during the pre-trial stage and I abide by it now - that the level is very low. In another situation, this should have made me happy, but this is history. This is the International Criminal Tribunal and not just anyone can take part here, either as Prosecution or Defence or as a Judge. The Security Council has established this Tribunal, and it is creating history. Whatever is said in these courtrooms will be creating international law. I acted as defence counsel in several hundred murder cases. Some were acquitted, some clients were found guilty. But if I look back on my life, I don't think I've done anything very significant in helping some of these murderers, but this is something else. And a very high level of evidence is required here, a very high level of logical argument. It's not about a drunk driver, you know. I called witnesses who were participants in the events, and that's the whole point. Bulatovic was the prime minister. The minister of foreign affairs signed the agreement with Geremek, and I expected Geremek to appear here if anything that Mr. Jovanovic said was incorrect, not low-level observers of the United Nations. They never probably even saw the agreement and yet they spoke about what was in it. Now Geremek has been killed in a traffic accident. When I spoke under Rule 92 bis, I mentioned a few persons who I thought were indispensable as witnesses, and I still think so. I'm grateful to the Court for selecting at least four. I can enumerate another ten now that I feel would have to be called. Two of them we didn't manage to get here, but had we done so we would have had everyone from Rambouillet, not just Mr. Petritsch, but also Hill and all the others, and we would have known exactly what happened in Rambouillet whether we like it or not. The judgements of history does not depend on personal interests. My personal interests as counsel is to get my client off; but when I come home, I know that my personal feelings sometimes differ from my professional attitude. All the participants should have been called here. In my system, when that is the conclusion reached by the court, it re-opens the case so that all the necessary witnesses can be called. There are no grounds for this under the Rules, but I would be happy if you were to do this because I've seen quite a few misunderstandings between the OTP and us. Well, let me begin with the following: We might have got Hill and the others here had the OTP wanted to call them. Had America wanted, we could have had Hill here. We could have had Ambassador Keller if France had agreed. I tried but he got married, and his wife wouldn't let him come here I assume. Look at the notebook of General Obrad Stevanovic which has been mentioned here, only one page of it. General Obrad Stevanovic, if it's true that he was in command of the PJP -- well, I don't know if the Prosecutor is -- well, it doesn't matter. But why was General Stevanovic not brought here to explain this? Later on, I'll deal with this, and you'll see some odd things in this notebook. I think, and this is my main objection, that for a reason I cannot fathom, there was not the will to call certain witnesses, whether out of fear, because the ones that were called did not say things the way they are presented in the indictment. Maybe they were afraid of that, but it would have been better had we seen and heard them. Because from his notebook we could have established, you see it says here something about the president and there's something before that and something after that, and he could have explained in what way he took the notes, who attended, who said what. That's P1898. Maybe I'm saying too often that this is a historical trial, but let's look at the example of Georgia.
