According to the same logic, as an American diplomat so picturesquely said, the Russians are using a hammer, and now this is going to be done in Georgia but not by NATO. Now they say that Saakashvili did have the right to enter his rebel provinces, but my colleague, Mr. O'Sullivan, explained all this brilliantly. And one of the reasons for the low level of evidence we've seen here is to avoid such comparisons. Let me just quote Obrad Kesic, a witness not mentioned by the OTP. He's an America, a member of the Democratic party, and he testified to a conversation with President Bill Clinton, regardless of whether Bill Clinton was in his honest or dishonest phase at the time. And Clinton said why Rambouillet hadn't been signed, that they had done everything so that Milosevic wouldn't sign. They wanted to have air-strikes against Serbia. And if you read Kesic properly, you can see that Holbrooke overstepped his authority in a way by signing the October Agreement, thus delaying the air-strikes until March, and his credibility has not been challenged by the Prosecutor. And, finally, I'm raising issues from the theory of criminal law. You know that one of the major principles is the principle of directness. The Court has to see and hear direct evidence. There is a joke from Roman times: How did they teach law? What's the difference between a witness, an expert, and the court? The witness saw but doesn't know; the expert knows but didn't see; the court neither saw nor knows but has to reach a judgement. It's a joke from ancient Rome. It's better for the court to see and to know than to read inserts from one witness or another. I consider that evidence presented directly before this Court has far greater weight than in another case, even if the witness unfortunately died. Look at these other cases, how did Prosecutor Nice coerce witnesses into giving statements? He made three or four attempts, put leading questions during the examination-in-chief, which is inadmissible but there was no Defence counsel. Slobodan Milosevic was not counsel, and it seems that he didn't really understand the law quite well. And the same happened with General Vasiljevic. He was given documents to read which he had never seen before, so what can you conclude from that? Things were suggested to him, and he was asked to read documents he knew nothing about. Look at Obrad Stevanovic's notebook, he commented on what he read there, but he never saw the notebook or attended the meeting and then that became evidence. I welcome the decision of this Chamber on page 26772 when General Dimitrijevic was being heard, where the Chamber said they didn't want witnesses to comment on others' letters, the parties would do that, and the Chamber would reach its assessment of that. And that is something I agree with. The following principle not being upheld here is in dubio pro reo, which is the basis of human rights in criminal proceedings. If in doubt, then do what is in favour of the accused. But the OTP is basing its entire indictment on suspicions only based on this or that quotation without any valid evidence, especially in the war period, 1999. Then there's another principle, your Anglo-Saxon principle, in support of this defence and that's beyond reasonable doubt, that's narrower than in dubio pro reo. If no one mentions that in 1999 Sainovic was a member of some sort of Joint Command, let alone a commander, if nobody observed that the chains of command of the army or the MUP included someone called Sainovic, if witness Djakovic whose notes you used as evidence explained that "ZK" was an internal term between him and Pavkovic when there was civilians and this implies Pavkovic and Lukic in 1998, what is this if not reasonable doubt that Sainovic was not a member nor was he in command of the Joint Command. And it hasn't even been proved that the Joint Command existed in the way described in the indictment and in the war period when crimes were committed. This may not be reasonable doubt, it's even worse than that. It's lack of any sort of evidence, whether written or oral. Justice must win, you know. You know that you were told here, "fiat iustitia, et pereat mundus," "let there be justice, even if all else perish." That is the principle on which we live, not hearsay. What did we hear in the Prosecutor's oral presentation of his closing arguments? They added a few new terms to describe Sainovic which are not present in their closing brief. If you have no evidence, then you have terms to use. If no one saw something, well, add a few adjectives and it may sound all right. For the first time we hear Sainovic's role described in a way that differs in essence from the way they're described in the indictment, the pre-trial brief, and in the course of the trial. For example, it said that Sainovic's role was to exercise political control over -- on page 26834, we never heard this before. And on the same page, the Prosecutor says that Sainovic was not directly involved in the chain of command of the VJ and the MUP and then to describe his role uses the term political control. On page 26841, he says that Sainovic's role was the role of a political director, political operative; two new terms again. For the first time in his closing brief, the Prosecutor describes Sainovic as a political director, as a person who exercises political control over the forces of the SRJ, both the army and the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija. Let me remind you that in paragraph 46 of the indictment, it said that Sainovic as the person at the head of the Joint Command commanded the forces, but now it seems he didn't command them but rather exercised political control. Characterizing Sainovic's role as that of a person exercising political control in my view affects the indictment against Sainovic essentially. It's not the same thing. This description, as I said, is contained neither in the indictment nor in the pre-trial brief. In these proceedings, I did not defend Sainovic from charges that he was a political director or a person exercising political control. Had I seen that this was how the Prosecutor saw him, I might have adduced other evidence in order to establish who in Kosovo and Metohija exercised political control over the security forces, on the basis of what regulations and with what results. Whatever the SRJ or Serbia was like, it was a state; and in a state, it is governments that exercise such control. In the situation that existed, the SRJ government controlled the army and the Government of Serbia, and the minister of the interior exercised control over the MUP. A slide was shown, for example, and this was something that was new as well, the first slide. What can we see there? Sainovic as someone who is superior to the Temporary Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija, and that was that. No evidence adduced at all. You have loads and loads of transcripts without Sainovic appearing anywhere; it was Andjelkovic. There was a mix-up with the names. Another statement that was made orally, the Prosecutor said that Sainovic was Milosevic's political left hand for Kosovo. The Prosecutor claims that this was something that was generally well known. There was evidence adduced that Sainovic was Milosevic's political confidant, but this is not something that the Defence knows or understands. This was certainly not something that was commonly known as the Prosecutor claims. How does this tie-in with the fact that is beyond challenge? I believe throughout 1999 during the war, we have evidence of a single encounter between Sainovic and Milosevic, and that was Vasiljevic's evidence before this Court, and there were other meetings with more people taking place, a confidant. Had he been some such, he would have spent every single day with him; but during the actual bombing, Sainovic wasn't there. They didn't see each other, they didn't meet, and that's why the Prosecutor dropped the charges about Milosevic ordering certain things through Sainovic. So what is the Prosecutor doing here? They posit a fact that they believe to be commonly known as they say. They take that fact and try to use it to create evidence instead of doing what they should do, what any Prosecutor should do. They should use commonly known facts and not merely state them but prove them. Once these facts have been proven, only then can conclusions be drawn based on these same facts; that is how it should be done. If there is someone who exercises political control, as the Prosecutor claims Sainovic did, then there must be some reports on any control exercised, and just on whose behalf. But we've seen no such thing. It's not in evidence, there was nothing in writing about that, and nothing was orally presented to corroborate these claims. I have not seen a single report by Sainovic to Milosevic about the situation in Kosovo or to anyone else for that matter. We have something that Sainovic said at the VSO meeting on the 25th of December, 1998. This is something that stems from his visit to a border post, which is a visit that occurred, as the Prosecutor mentioned, in the spring of 1998. That was the only thing that I found where Sainovic said anything about that at all. The Prosecutor said something new during their closing argument. Now, Sainovic and the Joint Command were used by Pavkovic as a pretext for his actions, and Milosevic purportedly enlisted the assistance of Sainovic in order to achieve his goal, for Pavkovic to be in charge of all the forces in Kosovo and Metohija. This is at 26892. Another allegation that I'd never heard before. This is yet a new creation by the OTP. The description of Sainovic's purported role -- this description of Sainovic's purported role is something that in no way follows from what the Prosecutor claims is their source, the evidence of General Dimitrijevic. He never says a word about Sainovic, especially not as related to any potential relations between Pavkovic and Milosevic. Again, this is merely an insinuation, yet another one, not to say a fabrication. There is nothing in evidence to show that Sainovic at any time did anything like that or offer any support to Pavkovic at all. I tried to decipher the OTP's need to come up with these concocted terms and qualifiers, and the only distinction that I was able to reach was the difference between Sainovic and the other accused in terms of his political role and function in the SRJ. He was one of the five deputy presidents. Carla del Ponte in her book says that one of those would not be allowed to be indicted by the Americans, but this book was never used in this trial. He was one of the five deputy presidents, but he can't place him at the scene, unless there is something new there, there is something new emerging. All right. We have no evidence. Let's try using qualifiers and adjectives: Political director in charge of this, in charge of that, director of this, director of that, and so on and so forth. Finally, it must be clear that any Trial Chamber could only reach a verdict based on facts in evidence. As God reigns in heaven, the Trial Chamber must reach a verdict on oath, but God must not submit any statement of reasons to anyone. And this is something else we heard from the OTP; they are asking the Chamber to do something. They say that there shouldn't have been any trial at all in the first place or any evidence for that matter. What we needed to do was accept any written statements that already existed at the time the trial began. So what have I spent the last two years doing? Why have I spent the last two years doing? Why have I been preparing for all of this if it's all no matter at all? We have these witness or those witnesses, we have the indictment read out, then a witness appears, and that takes care of a problem. Unfortunately, that's not a way we can do this. The Prosecutor asks you to use certain records, certain transcripts, certain documents which they then manipulate, and I'm about to show just how. But when the persons who actually produced these documents and the words contained in these documents are presented here and they say directly that what this was about, and the Prosecutor simply comes up with something else, what they are telling us now is simply not they way it was. It is the way I say it was. That's what they are telling us. You have General Dimitrijevic, General Djakovic, and this applies to both of these cases. Why would we need ten different explanations for this drunk driver. Let's take Djakovic and the problem is solved. That explains the Joint Command, I suppose, but we have no serious political analysis being performed in relation to the clashes in Kosovo and Metohija. We have Merovci's assessments and he is nothing but a mere body-guard or another interested party. Then Milosevic is being quoted, No one must beat you; and then the notorious Sana [phoen] memorandum which is not in evidence in this trial. It's not at memorandum either, it's a document that was prepared, and it's not notorious to begin with, but I suppose that none of that really matters, that the vision to keep Kosovo within Serbia is cited as a serious violation. But this is something that was being done again by this new government, and each government to come will probably be adamant about this just as well. I suppose such time will come as well. The change to the ethnic make-up, that's another thing that was mentioned. How is it possible to make a serious assertion of that nature to expel 800.000 people and just wait leaving these people outside? Because that is the only way to change the ethnic make-up, but they keep coming back, all too often in fact. Well, are the Serbs supposed to march straight into Washington for this to be achieved probably led by the Joint Command and Sainovic? Do you think we are really that insane in our country of Serbia to expect to achieve a victory like that? We just lay low waiting for the bombs to stop falling. We had a grand total of three electrical transformers that were in full working order in all of Serbia, and witness Milanovic said that. If they'd hit one of those three, all of our children would have ended up dead. A historical approach, a serious one, would show that the Albanians wanted to leave Serbia and they may have been right for all I know, or maybe they weren't right but for a hundred years. Certainly not. Look at Rugova, now he wants a republic. He wants to join Albania, he wants independence, as Thaqi does. It's all the same really, but that's what Serbia has been asking for, for a hundred years, way before Milosevic appeared, and it still wants all these same things. It also wants its own government administration. We've always wanted independence for ourselves. That's what I'm telling you. You see, this is simply not a right, this is simply not appropriate. Serbia is being accused because a company was doing drills near Podujevo. At the same time, there was NATO involved, and this is something that a witness told us to gather intelligence, that Kosovo's independence is being promised. And this is something that Mr. O'Sullivan raised, that members of the Kosovo Liberation Army are being bank-rolled, they are being given weapons. Yes, perhaps I should slow down. I apologise to the interpreters. Serbia is being accused because there was a company who was doing drills around Podujevo. At the same time, there was a massive build-up of NATO forces. It was making operative use of the intelligence. They were promising independence to the Albanians, they were training and bank-rolling members of the KLA. The NATO brigade arrives in Skopje, it arrives at the border, ship carriers entering the Adriatic sea. Small units are being brought in battalion size in order to defend in March 1999 on the eve of the war itself, and this is something that is seen as a violation of the agreement and then the war begins. What were we supposed to do, leave all our army back in barracks and once the bombing began leave all our children to die? We knew the war would start. We could see that for ourselves. We'd known that since October 1998 because threats were being made. This deployment by the VJ that occurred at the time proved to be the right one, because despite the massive scale of the bombing and the all-out attack by the KLA and their newly formed brigades, the land incursions were prevented from Albania and from elsewhere into Serbia, and these operations were foiled. To ignore these facts and to say the objective was to expel the Albanian population is simply something that is a non sequitur. Is this not sufficiently explained by the actions at Drenica and Malisevo? It is simply untrue to say that actions were being planned on the ground simply because the Prosecutor says there were the greatest concentration of the Albanian population in those areas. It is untrue that actions were being planned in that area because that was the area with the greatest concentration of the Albanian population. This area contained hardly 15 per cent of the Albanian population which was a minority. And this is simply untrue, it's inaccurate, this is a case of manipulation. If you look at that area, and this is obvious if you look at KLA documents, we had a KLA formation in that document and also foreigners from the Kosovo Verification Mission, and they were visiting their units there. Then we have Zyrapi's evidence, and then Defence witnesses brigade commanders Delic and Savic. If we take that evidence, we see what the extent of the clashes was and the extent of the area where these clashes were unfolding to VJ brigades and the KLA on the other side. Only then can a conclusion be drawn as to why the civilians were running and, the civilians running included half the Serbian population in Kosovo. We had Sandra Mitchell's evidence to show that. So the ethnic balance remained the same as before because 700.000, the Albanians before and the Serbs before, where again you have the same ratio. So what was achieved; the only difference being the Albanians came back, the Serbs never did. We still have over 100.000 Serbs living elsewhere because they have no homes to go back to. We have all sorts of random theories being put forward and then being transformed into facts. Sainovic at the head of the ZK. He approved all the decisions, he approved all the actions, and then the VJ commanders and the MUP commanders were advising him. How is it possible for something like this to come up again? We're all trying to show that Sainovic was positive in the way he discussed these matters as regarded the withdraw all the forces, the legality, the order, the work, his insistence that all crimes be punished and investigated. These are simple incriminations. What was he supposed to do? Just keep his mouth shut? He wasn't there for that. He was the deputy prime minister. He had to say something and he said all the right things, for the crimes to be punished, for the troops to be withdrawn pursuant to the agreement that was reached. Now, all of a sudden the Prosecutor is twisting all these things as something that is not in favor of Sainovic. They are using this as an incrimination against Sainovic, so I can't help but wonder -- well, I may be going a little beyond my brief right now. During the sentencing part of the closing arguments, they talked about aggravating circumstances. Is it possible for a group of six people not to have a single mitigating circumstance in their favor? Okay, so they say Sainovic was guilty in relation to the period in the indictment. Is it so difficult to say that by Rambouillet he was fighting for peace and then he might as well killed himself later on, he might have resigned, and then we could see what happened, but at least give him his due. You've got to hand it to him. He made sure that an area, God knows where, I no longer remember where, now had electricity. So this turns out to be another crime that he committed. Is that possible? Coordination between the MUP and the VJ. According to the Prosecutor, this is something that is foul. Mr. Naumann said that this was something that had to exist during a time of war because of friendly fire and for all sorts of other reasons at all. Now this seems to be tantamount to coordinating crimes, the examples of Suva Reka, Mala Krusa, Izbica, Milosh Giliq street in Djakovica are given. Sainovic is the deputy prime minister of the federal government, he is also the president of the Kosovo cooperation commission. This man perhaps knows something that any state official knew. All of us knew what was going on in general terms in Kosovo. Now suddenly it seems that this was just because he was receiving instructions from someone. There were a total of 15 actions carried out by the VJ and the MUP under the heading Joint Command, yet there were over 500 individual clashes. This is not the entire war as the Prosecutor claims, 500 individual clashes, which is something that General Lazarevic confirmed as well. Another fact that is neglected is the fact that internal relations in the VJ, on the one hand, and the MUP on the other, disciplinary action, criminal action being taken against members of the human resources. This isn't something that was being coordinated. That's never mentioned at all. All they are mentioning are some actions but this is of vital importance in terms of Sainovic's responsibility as seen by the Prosecutor. He should have all of that, he should have people coordinating his personnel policies, he should have people coordinating disciplinary actions that were being taken. In their final brief, they see the Joint Command in 1999 as comprising four persons: Pavkovic, Lukic, Lazarevic, and Sainovic. That's what the Prosecutor is telling us in his final brief. Now in his closing arguments, we see that Sainovic did not necessarily have to be in Kosovo. It wasn't us who said in our brief that Sainovic had been in Bor throughout, as you suggest. What I said was that among other things, he spent some time both in Bor and in Belgrade and in Ilidza -- or in Vinca and in Vares during the war; but how, then, could he have exercised command over this Joint Command from such a great distance. If you try to use simple logic, this cannot stand. In their closing argument, the OTP say that the joint criminal plan came into existence at the latest by October 1998, and they relate this to something that Milosevic told to Naumann: "Next spring, there will be a final showdown with the Albanians like the one in Drenica in 1945 and 1946." First of all, the witness has no clue what occurred at Drenica, and this is something that the witness shared with the Trial Chamber with no hesitation. Defence witness Veljko Odalovic explained that this was a showdown which [indiscernible] as Albanians. They were armed Albanians, members of the -- of Hitler's coalition. What can this possibly have to do with forced removal of the Albanian population or any expulsion or part of any plan such as seen by the OTP? This was a case where a gang was being liquidated, done away with. It's not people or civilians being expelled or driven out. The Prosecution then starts to develop a thesis, but it seems to have given up on that already, according to which Milosevic and the others wanted to see the bombing of Serbia to be able to put their plan into effect; and so in Rambouillet what happened happened. Now, how can anybody believe that, that somebody would be ready to be in favour of having a whole country bombed by NATO? Subotica was bombed thousands of kilometres away from NATO. They hit where they could, not only Kosovo was hit. What person would enter into a conflict with the largest coalition that exists in the world today, a conflict and clash which they know full well they cannot win? Now, I accept what my learned colleague and friend Mr. O'Sullivan said and the way he explained the situation in Rambouillet and who orchestrated Rambouillet, but I'd like to add the testimony of Witness Kesic as well to that. Now, while we're on the subject of Rambouillet, I have to say something because I am Sainovic's Defence counsel. I have to say something about the person that Sainovic is and his role in Rambouillet, and I would like to rely on everybody who was called as a witness, Petritsch, for example, and all the others. Did their words not show the operative quality of Sainovic, his desire for peace for example? How many times did he go in and out of Rambouillet? Whenever he needed to says the Prosecutor, he went to see Milosevic. I never saw that. The witnesses spoke about one time he left to consult Milosevic, but here we suddenly have multiple times. And when they say that he left, it was to save the negotiations, they say. Well, is that to be held against him? Had he have refused to go, that would have seemed to have been a quality in their mind. Is it not quite clear that the order to bomb was given in October 1998? What was it called, an act or whatever, an order? And Holbrooke's agreement, the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, prevented that. That's not being challenged, not even the Prosecutor is challenging that, the act or the order. Important sections of the Army of Yugoslavia were in Kosovo and Metohija at the time. Many of them, it would have been much easier to engage in persecution then; and if they wanted bombs, well, Holbrooke should have been rejected then. Certain forces according to Kesic wanted to do that, and they criticised him for it. Then it would have been more -- it would have been easier to persecute people, but I never understood how the Prosecutor explains and interprets the plan and how you could prevent these people from coming back. That's what I'd like to know, unless we were victorious over NATO and beat NATO, and nobody in their right mind can think that that could be the case. But anyway, the bombing came to an end, peace in Kumanovo came, all this was over, and the resolution guaranteed that Kosovo was a component part of Yugoslavia, and the United Nations entered Kosovo and not as was demanded in Rambouillet, that we should sign up for an occupation of the whole of Yugoslavia by NATO. Jovanovic, Witness Jovanovic, spoke about all these details and the referendum which meant the independence of Kosovo as well. Let me summarize. How did the war begin in the first place? Holbrooke arrived and set an ultimatum. He said, "Sign Rambouillet," that would mean NATO's occupation, the referendum for Kosovo's independence, "or we're going to bomb you." And that was the reason for the bombing and the war, and this was explained by witness Kesic. And we know how the war ended, with a Security Council Resolution 1244, the sovereignty of FRY guaranteed. There's no occupation of the federal state, and the forces guarantee security to the Serbs. Now, how far that was put into practice is another matter, and it is essential to mention another detail that I wish you to bear in mind here. It is Sainovic's conversation with Rugova, and this is mentioned here, too, and the agreement they reached, what Sainovic told him: One, an end to the bombing; and, two, the return of refugees. The Serb refugees never returned, and the cease-fire was accepted, and that's what happened. This agreement with Holbrooke was respected; it was adhered to. You heard that here from the NATO representative and from other observers. Now, why would it have been respected if we had a criminal enterprise of any kind in mind? One assertion is being made here and asked why people didn't flee from Belgrade just like the Albanians fled from Kosovo. You can't compare the two; it's impossible to compare the two if you're serious. In Belgrade, for example, NATO, General Naumann, so on, it was by mistake that the Chinese embassy was hit. There were some mistakes, but they said they selected targets and tried to avoid civilian casualties. It's not that people didn't flee from Belgrade. People tried to take their wives and children to safety. Some politicians fled, so that did exist. But most people stayed put because there wasn't that much reason for them to flee. They expected the bombing to end every day, and they kept telling us over television, well, it's just a matter of a few days. Everything functioned, traffic functioned, there were power cuts, and so on, but electricity would return. And there was no fighting in the streets, the KLA hadn't entered Belgrade for there to be shooting in Terazije square, and so on. That's when the people fled, but like this they didn't. You know, this brings me to a hypothetical question, and I agree with Mr. Hannis that we shouldn't use any hypotheticals here, but envisage the situation. Had NATO decided to bomb Belgrade alone, only Belgrade, would 800.000 Albanians have fled from Kosovo? Why would they have? That's the answer to it. There you have it. Why would they have fled from Kosovo if they targeted Subotica, Belgrade, Novi Sad, et cetera? That's the best evidence and proof that it was because of the NATO bombing that they fled on any grounds. I have to respond to something the Prosecutor said in his question as to why we make a difference in our closing arguments, Mr. Stamp asked this, between 1998 and 1999 when it's the same thing. Well, the difference is in one point, and that is it's in the war. In 1999 we had war, in 1998 we had peace. NATO is the difference. So if we're talking about the Joint Command, whatever that means, in 1998 you have notes, you have meetings; in 1999 you have nothing, none of that, because none of that existed and Sainovic wasn't there at all. And that's the difference, that's the difference that I'd like to underline. There's no evidence, no proof, that civilians were present in the chain of command of both the army and the MUP, and that is why Sainovic was dislocated from Kosovo as the fourth member, the only civilian, and then I suppose commanded by remote control or whatever. The Prosecutor relies on P1317 exhibit. I think we've analysed that sufficiently. It's the one where we say that the Joint Command was thought up or established, whichever you like, by Slobodan Milosevic, and that's where the Prosecutor stops. However, we can go on discussing that document. It talks about handing over military documents to the secretary of the cabinet of Slobodan Milosevic, and that man's name was Goran Milinovic. And he is at liberty today walking around Belgrade; and as far as I understand it, no one ever asked him about that, at least not by the OTP he wasn't asked about that. I did ask him. Anyway, the documents were handed over at the time to the military cabinet of Slobodan Milosevic and then says when in October the Joint Command ceased. So this document says that it came into being but also ceased to exist at that time as well. A document is a document. If you're going to use it, then you must use it truthfully. We're talking about October 1998, because it is in that document, at the end of that document, that it says that the Joint Command ceased to exist, in October 1998; and then the military documents were handed over to the secretary of the cabinet of Milosevic, and his name is Goran Milinovic. Now, the next thing I would say to say this: The letter by Perisic is being treated in a completely erroneous manner when it comes to Sainovic. The Prosecutor fails to remember that we're talking about the word "attempt" here. At that time, according to the position taken by this Prosecutor, Minic was at the head of the Joint Command, but look at the date. Evidence shows that the very next day after this letter, Perisic issued an order and established a forward command post of the 3rd Army in Pristina which controlled and guided the work of the Pristina Corps. After that, Perisic -- or rather, in addition to that, Perisic on a number of occasions sent inspectors out to Kosovo, and he went to Kosovo and Metohija himself. All this after the letter without noticing anything untoward. It was normal that Sainovic was in command of the troops. Perisic stayed on for a few months as the head of the General Staff, Chief of the General Staff; after the letter, that is. Yes. I want to make a correction here. I don't think I said that. Perisic did not notice anything untoward, anything unnormal, and it would be not normal if Sainovic were to be in command. So we forget that after July, Perisic for several months to come was at the head of the General Staff, and nowhere did I see him mention Sainovic at all or involvement in the troops. And, finally, the Defence would like to stress that the Prosecution, except for the letter, did not wish to call Perisic as a witness. It said it didn't believe him. Geoffrey Nice said even worse things: "Why would I believe him, why would the Trial Chamber believe him, and why would we believe in the good intentions of the writer of the letter?" Next, the Prosecutor, once again, says that Sainovic's words at two meetings of the MUP were some sort of instructions or orders. All the witnesses that took part in the meeting - and we heard them all - state quite the reverse. So we cannot conclude that Sainovic is ordering anything, issuing any kind of orders, and we can see that he did attend both meetings for a brief period of time. He didn't even attend the meetings in its entirety, and he was the vice-president of the government not as a commander of a Joint Command or a political director or goodness knows what else. They say he said that the refugees should be registered, and that is taken to be an order. But if you look at the discussion that was held after his departure, you will see that the chiefs of SUP are reporting on how many people they'd already registered. So this was ordered earlier on by someone else and he just mentioned it. Vice-presidents receive instructions as to what they're going to say. He came as the vice premier, the vice premier of the government, to attend the meeting. And when the Jezerce action is mentioned, the same thing holds true. When Sainovic talks about this, we can see that the action is already underway and had been ordered well before; whereas, from what the Prosecutor says, it would appear that he ordered it. And quoting Vasiljevic is very often incorrect. Vasiljevic before this Trial Chamber never -- never in this court did Vasiljevic say that Sainovic was a member of any Joint Command. And when he speaks about the meeting held on the 1st of June, if you listen carefully to what he said, he said I don't know what Sainovic was doing over there. So, regardless, you now have two statements; two statements have been made. I expressed the concern, although I can't claim this for sure, that nonetheless Pavkovic's and Lukic's interviews will be used against the other accused in one way or another, because they are mentioned within the context of Sainovic by Mr. Hannis. I hope that this will not pass -- hold water with the Trial Chamber. And now something with regard to the founding and meetings of the ZK. I say they are my concerns, but I don't say that that's what's going to happen. If we look at the Prosecution brief and our pet subject, the notes which we call the meeting of the Joint Command, then the Prosecutor quotes some ten sentences, about a dozen or ten - if I have made a mistake I apologise - which allegedly Sainovic says according to Djakovic's notes. Now, look at one precise fact, you have 69 meetings in all. At each of them five or six people take part in the discussion, which means 400 various pieces of discussion, and Sainovic takes part in ten. How could I put this? I don't know how to tell you this. Had Sainovic been in command and had there been a command of any kind, then he would have had to have taken the floor for a great length of time. He would have had to issue orders, make conclusions, make observations. He would be the central personage, and that could have been seen from the notes, who issues instructions, orders, gives permission, and so on; whereas, he wasn't even able to get a helicopter from General Samardzic. So there you have it. And from sentences pulled out of context - and I repeat witness Djakovic explains just how valid his notes are; I don't need to remind you of that - then the conclusions are made that Sainovic was in command of the whole army and the MUP and, of course, throughout the whole time. Now, there's another interesting point. Djakovic confirmed that he kept the notes only when he was there; when he wasn't there, nobody kept any notes at all. So what kind of command is this I ask you? Whereas, in fact, this is how the voids between the meetings are being explained, the spaces between one and another. Djakovic was probably engaged elsewhere, the meetings were held in his absence, and nobody took notes. Does that sound to you like a valid command? And that's how these gaps are explained. You did not present a single document where Sainovic is mentioned as a member of any Joint Command, let alone that he was the commander of a Joint Command. Wherever mention is made of the vice premier or president of the commission for cooperation with the OSCE, Djakovic was brought in despite the Prosecutor, if I can put it that way. And he explained everything to us; and, of course, this cannot be found in anything the Prosecutor has presented to us. As far as the Prosecution is concerned, it never happened. Had he succeeded to bring Philip Coo as an independent investigator or analyst, whereas, he was an ordinary investigator of the OTP interviewing everyone - Vasiljevic, Lazarevic, Lukic - and putting in the Joint Command Sainovic everywhere, then the final brief would have been just Philip Coo because that's all they could have referred to, Philip Coo; but luckily they weren't successful in achieving that because he wasn't an independent expert, and, indeed, he was no expert at all. Did it escape your attention that everybody said that those meetings were held always after Pavkovic received orders from the generals? And if you believe Djakovic, then the coordination of the army and the MUP had been completed. Djakovic said that here. So who was in command then and who was in command of what? Because everything had been completed, everything was already over. So Pavkovic, after he received an order from Simic or Samardzic, met up with Lukic; they coordinated among themselves, among the army and the MUP; and only after that was that meeting held, and there were no further orders to be issued at that meeting because all orders had been issued already, and that's what Djakovic told you. Let's mention General Dimitrijevic's testimony who said that it was ridiculous to think that Sainovic was in command of the army, and I said it was sad because that's why Sainovic was here. What bothers me is that Defence witnesses are said to be not telling the truth. It's very hard for me to utter the word "lie." These people were never heard as suspects or anything else. With most of them, the OTP didn't even want to interview them, but let's look at the quality of the OTP witnesses. Who said something nice about Ljubinko Cvetic? We heard that he was not a good man, that he was a man who didn't do good work. What about Tanic? That state was attacking the state that he was a citizen of. Is that a moral man? As for General Vasiljevic, he was interviewed by Philip Coo as a suspect and was later promoted to the status of witness because probably his answers suited someone, but even he did not claim before this Court that Sainovic was either a member or the commander of the Joint Command. Let's look at the statement he gave to the Defence and his testimony before the Court. And, finally, I have to ask myself, if the Defence witnesses were not telling the truth, I have not read anything about the Court witnesses, I haven't heard anything about them. Does that apply to them too? Allow me, Mr. President, at this point to move on to the more boring part and read you the paragraphs where the Prosecutor misquoted what the documents actually say. Paragraph 21, the Prosecutor says that the basis of the Serbian nationalist policy was that the Serbs must live on territory controlled by the Serbs or else they will be exposed to discrimination, prosecution, and genocide. I cannot find any source for this claim. Paragraph 22, events in Serbia in the spring of 1987 are described based on statements by Merovci and Abrahams. The Prosecutor is simplifying all the important historical events and presenting them through the statements of witnesses who are biassed or who are not sufficiently conversant with the facts. Let us bring in a real expert and support this with proper documents and witnesses because it's a large claim. Paragraph 24, he says that Milosevic was in power for eight years and that it was imperative that he retain Serb control over Kosovo, and this is quoting Merovci. This is again a sad simplification of historical events, and it constitutes ignoring the reality of social and political affairs at the time. Kosovo was part of the sovereign territory of the Republic of Serbia, and the issue of control over part of the territory of the country was not a result of criminal intent, it was a constitutional obligation. How would you apply this to Georgia? Is Saakashvili guilty for wanting to keep his own territory, and are the Russians right then to fight him, or does this apply only to our people? The Prosecutor says, in paragraph 25, that at a meeting with Phillips, Sainovic said that the Albanian population did not wish to co-exist with Serbs to whom Kosovo belonged. The Prosecutor pulled this out of context. Sainovic was speaking in the context of his, Sainovic's, dissatisfaction with the terrorist activities in which part of the Albanian population was participating. In his notebook, 2D17 - and I ask the Court to pay attention to it - Phillips noticed that at a meeting on the 24th of November, 1998, Sainovic when asked by Walker why fewer and fewer Albanians wanted to live in Yugoslavia replied that the majority of the population in Kosovo and Metohija believed that there could be a political solution to the crisis. Phillips confirmed this in his testimony before this court. Look at transcript page 11879, and this has nothing to do with what the Prosecutor is claiming. Paragraph 26, the Prosecutor states that Milosevic ordered the establishing of the Joint Command, referring to an unsigned letter which the federal Ministry of Justice sent to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 12th of July, 2002. That's the document I've already mentioned, P1317. First of all, the letter isn't signed. There's no source quoted, no source mentioned, for its claims. Only claims are put forward according to the knowledge of the military organs. It doesn't say what organs or on what basis. The Prosecutor is using this document to show when and where the Joint Command came into being, but he doesn't use the other part of the document, only several lines, which says that the Federal Ministry of Justice informed them that the Joint Command ceased to exist in late 1998. There's no other evidence, so suddenly this correspondence from 2002 is put forward but only in part. And, again, there is mention here that military documents were handed over to the secretary of the office, and this is the best proof that there is no longer any command because if there are no documents it means it's over. Goran Milinovic, who is now undergoing criminal proceedings in Belgrade before the fourth municipal court as stated by witness Kostic who was heard here, but he told me this unfortunately after the trial. It's easy to check this in connection with these documents. I don't know what his defence is, I really don't. But it's very important to say here, and it's being ignored by the Prosecutor, that General Dimitrijevic explained in his testimony how this letter came into being. This is very interesting because Dimitrijevic denies the first half of the letter. In this same paragraph, 26, the Prosecutor states the following: The Joint Command had no other authority in law than what Milosevic transferred to it. But no source is adduced for this claim. It's fabricated, it's unprofessional, and its aim is to mislead the Chamber as if this was definitely the case. Paragraph 28, although the Serbs were a majority in Kosovo and Metohija, it says, many Serbs considered Kosovo and Metohija to be an integral part of Serbia. Well, it was part of Serbia, it wasn't many Serbs, all Serbs considered it to be part of Serbia because it was part of Serbia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The Serbs were a minority not a majority in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even in the Security Council resolution this is confirmed, and that's resolution 1244, although it wasn't respected by America. Paragraph 29, the memorandum of the Serbian academy of arts and sciences of 1986 is mentioned, and genocide over Serbs is mentioned. The memorandum was never completed, and it wasn't presented as evidence by the Prosecutor in this case so that you might see what is in it. And you can see that Abrahams didn't read it either, he didn't read that document, that's evident. This is all improvised, this is all superficial. It's copied from article 63 -- or rather, count 63. Paragraph 30, Baton Haxhiu is used as a source for the claim that Milosevic was used in Kosovo and Metohija in order to gain power. The previous statement is copied from paragraph 63 of the Prosecution pre-trial brief. This Baton Haxhiu was found guilty of contempt by this Court, and this shows you the quality of the witnesses called here. Paragraph 33, it says that the amendments to the Constitution of Serbia were adopted with the help of tanks, and the source of this claim is Rugova who was neither a delegate in the Assembly nor was he present at the session. So how can we ask him where he got this? And this all shows the weight of the evidence and the value of this evidence. Paragraph 36 says that Milosevic used his majority of the SPS Assembly in order to enact legislation and that he relied on selected loyal members of the SPS such as Sainovic, but again no source is given for this. Where did they get this? I don't know. They weren't even members of the Assembly, so how did he rely on Sainovic in the Serbian Assembly? I have no idea. Paragraph 43, this is again paragraph 73 from the pre-trial brief. Numerous witnesses spoke about the SPS session of the 16th -- paragraph 42, let me correct myself, not 43. Many witnesses spoke about the session of the 16th of June, 1998, and a sentence is extracted from the discussion there, but Sainovic never took the floor. Paragraph 43, again there's mention of Drenica, and the Veljko Odalovic's testimony is ignored completely. Naumann is mentioned, who admitted he didn't know what this was about and that he didn't manage to find it in the literature. Paragraph 48, this concerns orders issued by the Joint Command in relation to the non-Albanian armed population. The OTP claims that they provided support to the army forces and the MUP. We've heard several dozen testimonies here about the way in which this claim is found in the Joint Command orders. From General Lazarevic onwards, everyone explained that this was somehow automatic and that it simply didn't happen. Paragraph 57, the Prosecutor fails to refer to key documents on the basis of which the anti-terrorist action began, and these are the documents of General Perisic, directive and other orders. And as far as I can understand, he's not part of any joint criminal enterprise and yet it is based on his orders and directives that this happened. Paragraph 73, again the notebook is used but a part of it not written by Djakovic. And I abide by all the objections that we don't know who the author is and so on and so forth, but let's see how this is quoted. The words on page 162 of the English version: "When we withdraw, we have to be careful, we have to take care that nobody finds parts of certain detachments who have not withdrawn. There must be no discrepancy with the information already issued." So this is being interpreted as an attempt to conceal something; although, there is no mention of concealing parts of detachments nor is Sainovic doing this. Of course, the Prosecutor explains these words as Sainovic's order that parts of the detachments should hide; although, nowhere in the conversation mentioned in this notebook is there any mention of hiding parts of the detachments. Although all the other evidence in the case, including KDOM reports, NATO communiques, and Madeleine Albright's testimony, all this shows that the withdrawal was actually carried out. So Sainovic's words were quite the opposite of what the Prosecutor interprets them to be. Paragraph 74, the Prosecutor states that Sainovic was the only person authorised to permit the inspection of barracks because this was not in agreement with the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement. Jovanovic confirmed this; and as I said, nobody asked Geremek whether this was true or not. So the agreement is being explained by whoever wants to but not those who drew it up. Loncar testified before the Court that the federal government discussed the decision and that the decision of the federal government was not to allow inspection of the barracks because it was not in compliance with the agreement on the KVM, and that's on page 7601. Paragraph 81, the Prosecutor speaks of the concern of high-ranking VJ officers about the actions of the ZK in connection with the VJ; and Perisic's letter is quoted, P717, but Perisic nowhere mentions the Joint Command --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Joint Command, not ZK.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most that is said is a civilian part of the staff, but there is an operative inter-ministerial staff where Perisic did attend the meetings as did civilians, if one can trust the minutes. So how the Prosecutor concluded that this is the Joint Command is not clear; and other staffs are also mentioned, not just the Joint Command. Paragraph 107, from the instruction for the defence of built-up areas, it has the Joint Command in the title. And it says in the instructions that this is temporary and that the MUP was combining the activities. It doesn't say anywhere that these units were being subordinated to the MUP as the Prosecutor claims. Besides this, in the file, there is a testimony explaining the provenance of this document, P1065, which is entitled: Joint Command, instruction for the defence of settled areas, built-up areas. Djakovic testified that the document was created by an operative organ; that's transcript page 26416. Paragraph 120, the Prosecutor states, according to the Joint Command order for the defence of built-up areas, again this is exaggeration. It's not an order, it's an instruction, and that's not the same thing and the instruction is temporary. Was it ever applied? Nobody knows if it was ever implemented. How long did it last? We don't know that either, if it was implemented. There's no evidence in the case to show any of this, but an attempt is being made to extend this to the entire indictment. On the contrary, in August 1998, the MUP did establish a reserve police detachments, units, but nowhere was it -- was there command. In paragraph 156, there's no mention of any sources for these claims. I'm trying to speed up. Paragraph 156, the Joint Command was established in June 1998. The evidence is supposed to be the ministry letter. Djakovic says that he and Pavkovic made up the title. Do you believe him or not? Paragraph 157, the Prosecutor says: Pursuant to a decision by the Supreme Defence Council dated the 9th of September, 1998, the VJ made a plan to combat terrorism. Any reference to the Joint Command there? This is a planning function. Based on what the Prosecutor says, this is in Belgrade and not that the VJ, not with Sainovic, yet that is what the indictment claims. Paragraph 160, the first meeting of the Joint Command was held in Pristina the day after the meeting at Milosevic. This was the conclusion in the first entry in Djakovic's notebook dated the 22nd of July, 1998, but Djakovic, himself, said the term was used before the civilians arrived. This is at pages 26378 and 26381. Djakovic also explained who the term Joint Command was applied to, and this is page 26382. That is the explanation. If you want the truth, consider Djakovic. If you do, you won't need ten other explanations about things entirely unrelated to all of this. Paragraph 158 says that at a session of the Main Board of the SPS a group of three was appointed, and Milosevic observed that the group should be amplified, extended. In paragraph 160, the Prosecutor claims that Milosevic's request was met. At a meeting dated the 22nd of July, 1998, this extended group now included Sainovic, Pavkovic, Lukic, Gajic, and Djakovic. I don't know what the source is for this declaration, except for that the fact of the entire list of persons attending the meeting on the 22nd of July, 1998, is in Djakovic's notebook, P1468. How based on a list of those attending can one conclude that this was Milosevic's desire and that this was a way to see them implemented? I simply fail to understand that. There is no evidence showing this. There is a list of who Milosevic is dispatching. Why do we have nothing in writing about this apparent extension? Paragraph 161, now that's really interesting. The Prosecutor claims Djakovic was the note-taker for the VJ at these meetings of the Joint Command. For two years, the Prosecutor kept claiming that Djakovic's notes were records of the meetings of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Now they called him a note-taker. Let me repeat. Perhaps this was on account of my speed. Paragraph 161, we see the Prosecutor claiming that Djakovic was the note-taker for the VJ at meetings of the Joint Command, note-taker. For two years, the Prosecutor has been claiming that Djakovic's notes were records of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Now all of a sudden Djakovic is a note-taker only for the VJ. This is some progress in understanding his role. I see now the Prosecutor finally accepts that there are no minutes of any meetings of the Joint Command, but again we have something new cropping up. There is an oral explanation by the Prosecutor promoting Djakovic to a member of the Joint Command, claiming that he kept minutes in an official capacity which is another case of manipulation. Paragraph 162, claims that as of the 22nd of July, 1998, meetings of the VJ, the MUP, and, as the Prosecutor claims, Milosevic's officials from Belgrade were described, were designated as the Joint Command. This is corroborated apparently by Djakovic's words at 26378; however, at 26378, Djakovic never actually says that these meetings were referred to as the Joint Command. All Djakovic says there is that he and Pavkovic for internal purposes referred to as the Joint Command, while the politicians called these meetings sessions. Paragraph 163, the Prosecutor claims that these meetings were first held in the PIV building, the Temporary Executive Council building. In July 1988 [as interpreted], there is no Temporary Executive Council any longer, or rather, not yet. The Temporary Executive Council was only set up in 1998, in September 1998. Your Honours, I think this might be a convenient time for our lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Fila. Thank you. We will resume in an hour at quarter to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 163, the Prosecutor says that Momir Stojanovic became aware of the existence of the Joint Command in June 1998; however, at pages 19761 through 19762, where the Prosecutor makes this claim, the allegation is simply not to be found. Momir Stojanovic speaks about when he heard of the term "the Joint Command," which doesn't mean that he heard of the existence of a body called the Joint Command. This is particularly important because Stojanovic explains what he heard. He explains what he heard and what he heard was about. Kotur also says nothing about being aware or becoming aware of the existence of some command; rather, at page 20714, as the Prosecutor claims, he talks about the term "the Joint Command" and the explanation of that term provided to him by Djakovic. Kotur never says a single word about the command. He simply recounts what he was told by Djakovic about his conversation with Pavkovic and what to call the meetings that he attended. In this paragraph, the Prosecutor also mentions Ljubinko Cvetic, who allegedly heard something that no one else who was with the MUP ever heard as early as the 10th of July, 1998; and I must emphasize this, as early as the 10th of July, 1998, at a time when, if we bear in mind the allegation contained in paragraph 160, the Joint Command never even existed. This is 12 days earlier. Cvetic also knows that Sainovic is at the head of this Joint Command; whereas, the Prosecutor, himself, claims that up until at least the 14th of September, 1998, it was Minic who headed the Joint Command. Sainovic could not possibly have been the person that Cvetic had heard anything at all about. Paragraph 164, the Prosecutor claims that Milosevic exercised control over the Joint Command first through Minic. Not a single source is quoted to corroborate this. This is a fabrication and nothing else. Evidence on Minic's chairing these meetings is something that the Prosecutor finds in Djakovic's notebook. In footnote 408, they say that Minic remained chairman until the 14th of September, 1998. In that same paragraph, they go on to state that Milosevic later exercised control, just as before, but through Sainovic. Two sources are indicated: Perisic's letter and Cvetic's letter at 8078. This is another fabrication from beginning to end. Cvetic's evidence at 8078; Cvetic's evidence, that's 8078. At first, it was Minic who chaired the meetings; and if Minic continued to chair meetings until the 14th of September, 1998, how then do we have Perisic's letter dated the 23rd of July, 1998, being used as a source that Milosevic was exercising control over the Joint Command through Sainovic? Logically, this makes no sense at all. This is essentially nonsense and an untruth. Perisic's letter makes no mention of the fact that Milosevic was exercising control over the Joint Command through Sainovic, nor is there any reference that he first did this through Minic and now through Sainovic. The letter is dated the 23rd of July. The meetings of the Joint Command allegedly started on the 22nd of July. It follows that this is pure nonsense. The other source for this affirmation or assertion that Milosevic was exercising control over the Joint Command through Sainovic is Cvetic; this is at 8078. If you look at that page or any other page for that matter in Cvetic's evidence, this theory is never mentioned at all. Apparently, Cvetic heard who the members and the leaders of the Joint Command were at a meeting at the MUP staff of the 22nd of July, 1998. Cvetic names these members and says that Sainovic was at the head of the Joint Command. This is absurd because the Prosecutor claims that Minic chaired the body at least up until the 14th of September, 1998. In addition to this, Cvetic is -- Cvetic's allegations are denied by everybody else, Mijatovic, Jurisic, Adamovic. Also in the transcript from that meeting, there is no mention of that, 6D798, paragraph 164. The Prosecutor claims that in October 1998, Sainovic chaired a meeting of the Joint Command; again, no source is given. They go on to state that Sainovic at that time issued orders; all of this probably based on the notebook which is P1468, and all this despite Djakovic's evidence, all this in the face of dozens of witnesses who explained how anti-terrorist action was conducted and how control was exercised over these actions in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998. It is entirely unbelievable how the Prosecutor should take Djakovic's notebook and then, based on that, draw the conclusion that Sainovic headed the Joint Command, and yet not a single word is found about that in that very notebook, paragraph 146 -- 164. The last sentence is another example of a shockingly inaccurate interpretation of evidence. The sentence claims that Sainovic occupied the position of head of the Joint Command throughout the period relevant to the indictment. There is only one source, Aleksander Vasiljevic. We're talking about the Milosevic transcript, and we're talking about Vasiljevic's evidence in this trial, page 43 of Exhibit P2589. This is the transcript from the Milosevic trial. Nice wants Vasiljevic to interpret Pavkovic's letter dated the 25th of May, 1999. Vasiljevic, based on that letter, offers an entirely free interpretation of the position and the role of the Joint Command. Elsewhere in that transcript, nice uses 19 lines of the transcript, nearly an entire page. He gives a speech and explains to Vasiljevic what this is about, stating that Vasiljevic was looking at a document that pre-dated the period that he was able to give evidence about because that was before this became relevant. Then he quotes parts of Djakovic's notebook and leads him to certain conclusions. The Defence would like to quote the position of the Chamber in this case; this is TT26722: "Witnesses are not to be used in order to provide analyses or to read other people's letters, but in order to give us directly their knowledge or any other knowledge they may possess about the relevant circumstances." Here we see Nice insisting that Vasiljevic do just that and comment on Pavkovic's letter. Another source is Vasiljevic's statement dated the 14th of January, 2007, which is in contradiction to Vasiljevic's statement dated July 2007 and other statements made by Vasiljevic. Also up until the 27th of April -- or by the 27th of April, 1999, Vasiljevic is already retired. Vasiljevic tells us himself about the Joint Command throughout 1998. He knows Stojanovic. Vasiljevic also says that Stojanovic never told him anything about the Joint Command throughout 1999; page 8820. How, then, can the Prosecutor conclude anything at all that based on Vasiljevic's evidence about the existence of the Joint Command at any point in time during 1999? Paragraph 166, the Prosecutor inaccurately represents Pesic as a source for the assertion that the Joint Command exercised command and control over the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo; this is P2502, paragraph 32. All that Pesic actually claims there is that the Joint Command coordinated the work of the VJ and the MUP, which is entirely different from what the Prosecutor would have us believe. Also, if we go to Cvetic's evidence, pages 8051 through 8052, there is no indication at all of what the Prosecutor would have us believe. If you look at pages 8194 through 8195, pages invoked by the OTP, Cvetic makes this even more explicit. The Joint Command coordinated activities, but the chains of command enshrined in the relevant laws were preserved in their entirety. Vasiljevic is mentioned in that paragraph, yet he knows nothing about the Joint Command. He knows no more than he was told by Stojanovic in relation to 1998, and this is something that we have already discussed. Paragraph 167, the Prosecutor tells us that the most important part of the activities of the Joint Command was the planning and coordination of the joint actions of the VJ and MUP in Kosovo. No source is given yet again. In that same paragraph, the Prosecutor says that Djakovic explains that the Joint Command was an element of coordination between the VJ and the MUP. Here the Prosecutor invokes Djakovic's evidence, but Djakovic's sentence was pulled out of context because the essence of his sentence was that the fact that the term "Joint Command" referred to Pavkovic and Lukic and no one else. Paragraph 171, the Prosecutor says that in P2166, page 3, we see that the Joint Command was in charge of implementing the plan for the suppression of terrorism. Quite simply, that's not what the document or that specific page say. There are no references at all to the Joint Command. The words "Joint Command" are not mentioned on that page at all. The Prosecutor quotes extensively the excerpts from Djakovic's notebook; although, the substance of this notebook has not been clarified, it has not been translated, and it remains illegible. Paragraph 171, the Prosecutor mentions armed civilians and the Joint Command. Quite aside from their inaccurate quotes of the document, there is something that is even more important that is being overlooked here; they're not being specific enough in terms of the time-line. What is 1998 and what is 1999? Paragraphs 172 and 173, the Prosecutor ignores the substance of a VJ document showing that the Pristina Corps was -- only carried out orders of its superior command -- exclusive role of the chain of command by the VJ. Paragraph 171, the Prosecutor furnishes as proof of the existence of the Joint Command, the plan -- or rather, the communications plan P1052, where we find the code-name Pastrik. However, the Prosecutor ignores evidence to the fact that Pastrik was a code-name used for the Pristina Corps, paragraph 179. The Prosecutor claims that the Joint Command is receiving directives from Belgrade, more specifically from Milosevic. The source of this is Vasiljevic, page 139, P2589. We find nothing about this there. Again, the Prosecutor refers to P1468, pages 63 through 64. 75, 130, no reference there either. Least of all do we get to understand what these documents really claim. Paragraph 179 mentions that the Joint Command issued a report and a conclusion about the implementation of the plan to combat terrorism in October 1998. They say that this is at P1011, page 72; again, there is nothing there, the document doesn't exist. There is just a heading, no more than a heading, indicating the existence of that report. But does that report exist? What does it say? Who produced it? No evidence on that. Paragraph 181, meeting dated the 29th of October, 1998. The Prosecutor entirely neglects assessments by Dimitrijevic and other participants in that meeting as well as their conclusions about what the minutes of that meeting really mean. None of the participants mention anything about the first stage of the Joint Command's work as quoted by the OTP. If we look at the conclusions of that meeting and based on this very document, P2166, we find nothing about the decision being taken at the meeting that the Joint Command should continue its work. Dimitrijevic's evidence denies the existence of any minutes or any transcript, that's P2166, because Dimitrijevic, himself, gave evidence to the effect that Susic was seated right next to him. No records were made of the meeting or else he would have seen it himself. Dimitrijevic also expressed his doubt to the effect that the record might have been produced at a later date under suspicious circumstances. We would also like to remind Trial Chamber of the fact that Minic tells us that he never used the term "the Joint Command." Paragraph 193, based on a plurality of several hundred documents used in this trial, in addition to the Joint Command order explained by Defence witnesses, the Prosecutor sets aside another two documents, P2016 and P2017, telling us that these documents prove the existence of the Joint Command during the war. The Defence believes that if at all the Joint Command had played a role attributed to it by the Prosecutor, there would need to be an incomparably greater number of documents telling us about its composition and telling us about its exact role in what was going on. Paragraph 194, the Prosecutor claims that it is possible to conclude that there is a parallel structure between the PRK, the Pristina Corps, as a staff of the Joint Command and the staff of the Supreme Command, but the sources being quoted there tell us nothing about that. Paragraphs 203 and 204, we find there a description of the meeting held on the 1st of June. Vasiljevic tells us clearly that he is not saying this is a Joint Command meeting; and what's more, he has no idea in what capacity Sainovic appeared at that meeting. If we go back to his notebook, and his notebook is shown, it doesn't say Joint Command meeting. It says a meeting was held at the Pristina Corps command; that's what it says. Paragraph 203, Vasiljevic is inaccurately quoted there. Vasiljevic allegedly says, "Do as we planned"; whereas, Vasiljevic's statement, and this is particularly important Vasiljevic's statement, P2600, paragraph 81, shows this, "Do as you planned." There's a world of difference there. Sainovic is not involved in the planning. This is a dangerous and inaccurate assertion, not to say capricious. Paragraph 262, the Prosecutor tells us who the members were of the Joint Command in 1999. They give us four names, but it is hard to see just based on what the Prosecutor drew this conclusion. We leave this open. Paragraph 281, the Prosecutor concludes that Stevanovic in his notebook recorded that in May 1999, he had together with Sainovic attended a meeting at Milosevic's. The source for this is a document that is being alleged to be Stevanovic's notebook, and this is concluded based on Vasiljevic's evidence; whereas, Vasiljevic first set eyes on this notebook when it was shown to him by the Prosecutor, Mr. Nice. Vasiljevic said explicitly he didn't know whether Sainovic had attended that meeting or not, and he didn't know whether he had contributed anything at that meeting or not. This is TT8830. If Stevanovic had testified in this trial, he probably would have been able to explain how and why he used special channels to set apart the transcripts of his meetings at Milosevic's from his own notes where he refers to Sainovic. I think we should now look at page 88 in the Serbian. This is 106 of the English, and the exhibit is P1898. This will help us better understand what I'm talking about. If Stevanovic had testified, he would have explained about the lines on these pages which obviously separate the body of the notes from the meeting with the president from perhaps some other text mentioning Sainovic. Can that please be displayed now so it's there for all to see. This is P1898. This is 88 in the Serbian and 106 in the English. Is it a problem for us to show this now? Could we please show the entire page in the Serbian, and then later we can have a look at the English just to clarify what I'm talking about. There. That is what I've been trying to say. You see item 8. It says "change of staff" or something along these lines, and then two lines drawn there, and then it says "chairman" and then whatever it says, and then the two lines end and they move on to item 9. Item 8 is followed by item 9, and that's probably what it says. So why is this being marked out? There are some strange recordings there, some strange numbers 306 or whatever. I have no idea what that means. But what this means is we can't take Vasiljevic's interpretation at face value, and Vasiljevic's interpretation does not allow us to draw any conclusions as to what this means. Does Sainovic ever attend this meeting? Is this the meeting we're talking about? If the Prosecutor had been interested in learning the truth, they would have brought Stevanovic to testify. That's all I'm trying to say, and we can stop here. I'm moving on to paragraph 660 where the Prosecutor says that Sainovic was the political leader of the delegation in Rambouillet. It's true that Sainovic was the only member of the delegation dealing with foreign policy issues, the rest were legal men or representatives of national communities. And from the evidence shown, it can clearly be seen that there was no political leader. All that existed was a delegation led by Professor Markovic. Paragraph 661 now, the Prosecutor states that Sainovic had influence in the socialist party of Serbia, first of all, as vice-president. Have you forgotten that as of the 24th of April, 1997, for example, Sainovic was not the vice-president of the SPS for reasons explained in detail in the Defence brief, and I don't want to repeat them here. Paragraph 662, the Prosecutor claims that Sainovic's influence emanates from his closeness to Milosevic. What are the sources? An excerpt from Bulatovic's book in footnote 1683 states -- or rather, Bulatovic makes no mention of Sainovic's strength emanating from his close relations with Milosevic. All that Bulatovic says is just one sentence, in fact. He says that Milosevic asked Sainovic to lead political activities with respect to Kosovo and Metohija, and Bulatovic goes on to explain that that was because Milosevic wanted to protect him, Bulatovic. Yes. That Milosevic wanted to protect Bulatovic. Does that speak about any closeness in relations? Quite the contrary, it speaks about the closeness between Bulatovic's close relations with Milosevic because Milosevic is protecting Bulatovic and sends this other man to Kosovo. Then, furthermore, it is stated, as a source we have Gajic on page 15443, that he also refers to this closeness in relations; however, that does not exist. There's none of that. The Prosecutor quotes two excerpts from Sainovic's interview as well about the affairs that Sainovic is engaged in. Once again, there's nothing about any closeness of relations from which his authority would be -- would emanate. Milosevic was the president of the state, and millions of people had contact with him -- or hundreds of people, and that quality was no different in character than the contacts and relationships Sainovic had with him. So I don't see how the Prosecutor can claim that there was a closeness in their relationships. Paragraph 662 goes further on and says that Sainovic was part of Milosevic's inner circle, which is an absolutely fabrication because nobody ever said that anywhere. I don't see it anywhere in writing or anywhere else for that matter. The Prosecution states that Naumann said that Sainovic was Milosevic's close associate. Naumann says that within the context of the meeting he had with Milosevic in January 1999 and with Sainovic and as the president of the commission. He quotes Petritsch; however, Petritsch speaks of the assumptions within the frameworks of the diplomatic community in Belgrade. Petritsch's description of the role of Sainovic is quite different, and the Defence provides it in exstenso in its brief. Paragraph 663, the Prosecutor begins with the following, and I quote: "As Milosevic's representative for Kosovo, neither in this paragraph or in previous paragraphs where such claims are made, nothing is said about what grounds this is based on," that Sainovic was Milosevic's representative in Kosovo. All the sources that the Prosecutor refers to in this paragraph relates to the time of the KVM, and at that time Sainovic had his obligations as president of the commission. And the Prosecution concludes on the basis of what Dimitrijevic says about what Crosland says. Crosland, Ciaglinski, and others speak of their assumptions and their impressions. They cannot know what the responsibilities were of the president of FRY and of Serbia because they didn't know the internal political system, all relations that governed the political system within the FRY and Serbia, for example. Ciaglinski says that Sainovic in 1999 -- that he saw Sainovic in 1999 every two or three days in Kosovo. Who, then, was in Rambouillet instead of Sainovic if Ciaglinski saw him in Kosovo so frequently? Paragraph 664, the Prosecutor says that whenever it was necessary to go -- for somebody to go to Belgrade, Sainovic went to Belgrade, and the conclusion made there is that he went every two or three days. Now, evidence has been shown and presented about that, yes, he did go to Belgrade but not on a daily basis. Paragraph 666, the Prosecution intentionally mixes up the time of the KVM mission with other times, and so they quote and say that Pavkovic and Loncar informed Sainovic about the events and uses Djakovic as a source. Loncar was speaking at one time; Djakovic's notes cover another time. So this is a mix-up of the time-periods, which serves the Prosecutor well in overcoming his basic problems, a time of war after the 24th of March, 1999. There are just a few indications about Sainovic's role in Kosovo and Metohija, and you can't have an analogy made there which is what the Prosecution wants to do to diminish the evidence and by using assertions and claims which refer to a different time-period. The Prosecutor also quotes Farkas as if he knew what Sainovic's role was in Kosovo and Metohija; whereas, Farkas, himself, says that from what Sainovic said at the meeting that was held on the 17th of May, 1999, he drew conclusions from which it is clear that he has no other knowledge than that, and that is to be found on page 16368. Paragraph 667, all the comments given by Sainovic at the meeting of the 17th of May, 1999, indicate precisely that Sainovic had -- did not have the role that the Prosecutor ascribes to him. Had Sainovic been responsible for Kosovo and Metohija, he would be the man who was asked all the questions and provided all the answers, the man who was given duties to perform, but none of that ever happened. Sainovic's participation at that meeting was marginal. Nothing that he said or did indicates that he had any authority, certainly not of the kind that the Prosecutor is ascribing. What the Prosecutor quotes as proof of Sainovic's influence on the basis of P2592 of General Vasiljevic's notebook is marginal and insignificant if compared to what the other participants at the meeting said when they took the floor. Paragraph 668, the Prosecutor talks about the confidence that Milosevic placed in Sainovic and says that it is evident that Sainovic had maintained contacts with Rugova, and he quotes Rugova and Merovci who says that he talked to Sainovic just to pass the time. There is no mention anywhere of Milosevic and the trust and confidence he placed in Sainovic. The Prosecutor also quotes Bulatovic, Jovanovic, Minic, Matkovic as sources for these claims; also fabricated. None of them makes any mention of Milosevic's confidence when it comes to Sainovic but exclusively the fact that Sainovic talked to Rugova and that those talks were important, nothing more than that. The Prosecutor, therefore, represents the facts inaccurately. Paragraph 668, the talks between Sainovic and Rugova in April 1999, the Prosecutor says that they were propaganda campaigns. There's no evidence of that. Rugova does not mention a propaganda campaign anywhere and neither does Sainovic. Paragraph 668, the Prosecutor claims that in Merovci statement, P2588, paragraph 64, we can see that Sainovic was acting in Milosevic's name and that he was consulting Milosevic before making decisions. Everything that it says in that paragraph is that Merovci saw Sainovic on television at some meeting which was also attended by leading officials together with Milosevic, and that's why hoe concluded that Sainovic was appointed by Milosevic. No other source bears that out. He also says Sainovic nodded his head when Merovci mentioned Milosevic; however, Merovci makes no mention of any decisions and who Sainovic consulted if anyone. He could not have known that.
