Everything that the Prosecutor states there has been construed by using parts of testimonies from witnesses, but they cannot be serious grounds for making any conclusions about Sainovic's role and his relationships with Milosevic. Paragraph 671, the Prosecutor states that on the 4th of May, 1999, Rugova and Merovci went to Belgrade for talks with Sainovic and Milosevic. There is no source for making these claims and assertions. They did travel to Belgrade to meet representatives of the Italian embassy, that is true, and to leave the country. Paragraph 673 begins with a flagrantly inaccurate assertion that the ZK started in June 1998 and existed until June 1999. There is no -- there are no grounds for this assertion because nobody said that at this trial at all. The next sentence is also inaccurate and incorrect. It says: "By Sainovic, Milosevic exercised control over the ZK." The source is Vasiljevic, P2600, paragraph 80. Vasiljevic presents his assumptions there. Even he who gives free interpretation to many things says that Sainovic must have been appointed by Milosevic. Now, in that sentence in Serbian is just a claim, an assumption. And even if you look at Vasiljevic's testimony superficially and even if you accept the fact that he knew something about Sainovic, these can only be assertions. Paragraph 673, the Prosecutor does not tell us how Sainovic at the material time of the indictment contributed to the preparation and planning of an action. All conclusions stem from Vasiljevic and his conclusion with respect to the meeting held on the 1st of June, 1999. Everything that Vasiljevic said -- what Vasiljevic said was that he did not know what role Sainovic played because Sainovic used what the representatives of the VJ said and MUP. There was no ordering, planning, authorisation of attacks, transformation of instructions, and so on and so forth. These are just claims made by the Prosecution and are not professional. Let me repeat, everything that -- all that Vasiljevic said was he did not know what Sainovic's role was and that Sainovic agreed with what the representatives of the MUP and VJ said. 2D383 [as interpreted] is the reference. No ordering, planning, or anything like that took place. All that has been construed and fabricated by the Prosecutor. Paragraph 672 [as interpreted], it says from the start of the ZK to the end of the war, Sainovic was the central figure in ZK activities, and then evidence follows. He was present at the session of the Main Board of the SPS, for example. In the previous paragraph, there's something different in the transcript. The number I quoted was 2D387 as a reference, 2D387. Anyway, he was present at the meeting of the Main Board of the SPS on the 10th of June, 1998, and on the 21st of July, 1998, at a meeting with Milosevic. Shall I begin again, paragraph 675, the Prosecutor states as follows: "Since the inception of the Joint Command up until the end of the war, Sainovic was the central figure in ZK activities, "and this is the evidence they offer up to support that assertion. He was present at the meeting of the Main Board of the SPS on the 10th of June, 1998; he was also present on the 21st of July, 1998, at a meeting with Milosevic where Pavkovic put forward a plan for an offensive. Sainovic, therefore, was the central figure because he was present at that meeting of the Main Board of the SPS with several hundred other people, might I add. And at the meeting, mention was made of Kosovo and Metohija, but Sainovic did not say a single word, nor did anybody mention him. And as far as the second meeting is concerned, there were many military, police, and political figures there, and there is no proof or evidence whereby Sainovic said anything or did anything. So how can he be a central figure if he only attended the meetings and did nothing more than that? Paragraph 676, the Prosecutor describes Sainovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, are you now just going to go through every one of these paragraphs of the Prosecution brief in relation to Mr. Sainovic's individual criminal responsibility, including repeating things you've already said in dealing with the Joint Command at the earlier stage? Is that what you're going to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try not repeat matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We observe your earlier comments, Mr. Fila, about Mr. Hannis's ten points of the drunk driver, but think that you may have fallen into the same trap to some extent. We also remind you that your opening gambit in your submissions was that if your case is any good, you won't have to say much about it as an advocate at the end of it. However, we do appreciate that what you're doing is analysing the Prosecution's submissions, and we actually find that a very helpful approach. But we would encourage you to minimise the repetition as far as you can. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 677 -- or should I skip that too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mustn't skip anything -- sorry. I thought you were asking me, but you're actually asking Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 678 -- believe me, I find this even more boring than you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the remaining part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a job to be done, that's all. I accept everything you say, Your Honours. I'll try to cut this short. Paragraph 678, this is about proving Sainovic's authority over the MUP. All I'm trying to say here is that there was a court order about only that part of the notebook being relevant which Djakovic interpreted at IC199. This is where Djakovic explains what the Prosecutor claims in paragraph 678. There is no mention there of any secretariats liquidations. I'm talking about pages 10 and 11 in the Serbian. The other piece of evidence on Sainovic's authority over the MUP is Merovci telling Sainovic that a part of the route was dangerous. The third proof is the question of the MUP's presence in Malisevo. Merovci said this was dangerous. That's it. I just said it like that. This is about the MUP's presence in Malisevo, the complexity that that part of the route was dangerous. And this is something that was explained by Byrnes and Phillips and the Prosecutor misrepresents this situation. I'm invoking Byrnes. Byrnes, he was working on that; and what he said Sainovic was doing, well, that's that, and it certainly wasn't authority over the MUP. 679, as if Dimitrijevic never gave evidence before this Court. Where is the principle of directness or immediacy and the right of any accused to a fair trial? 681, Sainovic's responsibility for the security situation in Kosovo and Metohija. This is proved by him attending several meetings in Kosovo, a grand total of two throughout the entire war, in fact. 684, paragraph 684, this is the best illustration of how worthless Djakovic's notes are. According to the OTP's interpretation, Sainovic is here saying on the 21st of September, 1998, that the Milosevic-Yeltsin agreement is not being implemented. It is entirely clear that Djakovic failed to understand or failed to record what was being said. The notes that do exist are obviously meaningless, especially to confirm the fact that the October agreement was being obstructed, and this is something that Sainovic was busy working on already as early as September. Paragraph 686, Sainovic tried to stop the inspection of the barracks; although, all the evidence we have says exactly the opposite. For example, 3D438, Obradovic says that he was informed by Sainovic that no inspection would take place, informed; and then Loncar said this was a decision of the federal government. The question of the helicopters of Malisevo, the electricity for the verification mission, this is something that was mentioned so many times there is no need for me to repeat this again, the conclusion being that Sainovic made no independent decisions at all. Paragraph 687, the Prosecutor says that Petritsch claims that Sainovic obstructed the Rambouillet talks. What I'm saying is this: The Court should take what Petritsch said at face value. If Petritsch said that about Sainovic, well, then, fine, but he didn't. Look at 10717, it's just not true. He says that Sainovic was a pleasant person to talk to and someone who was friendly and that he was someone that he was sending the Ministers Cook and Vedrine to speak to. Paragraph 688, the negative approach of the Serb delegation being a result of Milosevic's instructions. That may have been the case, it may not have been the case, but then the Prosecutor says that these instructions were forwarded by Sainovic. I simply fail to see that. They invoke Petritsch again who talks about these instructions but never mentions Sainovic. There is a reference admittedly somewhere, but he says probably from Milosevic but he is far from certain. Then Surroi, who here as was in the previous paragraph, is quoted. It's quite clear that he's in no position to know about the nature of those relations in the delegation itself, because as you know the Albanians and the Serbs never met, never physically met. They were physically separate during the talks. Yet, again, we go back to the previous paragraph, the now paragraph 688, what evidence do we have for Sainovic's behaviour? We see Dragan [Realtime transcript read in error "Sidran"] Milanovic's evidence being invoked there, but we don't know that this man said anything at all about Rambouillet. He talked about transformers, he talked about he the bombing of Bor, as long as we're talking about the same Dragan Milanovic. If not, then this was probably at a different trial somewhere where I was not present. Paragraph 688, the Prosecutor concludes that Sainovic had control over the delegation. It says Sidran Milanovic, not Dragan Milanovic. Dragan Milanovic. That is what it says. I have no idea who this man is. 688, Sainovic being in control of the delegation; no source quoted. 692, Tanic listens to a tape about Racko [as interpreted]. Tanic says he couldn't tell the voices and he couldn't really tell what it was that he had heard. He said it himself. Another allegation being made there is that Sainovic was supposed to punish some perpetrators or some such. Sainovic's authority to prosecute anyone, where does that come from? The Prosecutor himself tells us that both the VJ and the MUP had their own chains of command and disciplinary and criminal responsibility. What does Sainovic have to do with all this? Paragraph 693, this is something about the birth-rate among the Albanians, these are Milosevic's words, and then the conclusion by the OTP is this: Bearing in mind the close relations between Milosevic and Sainovic - and as I said to begin with, I have no idea how you arrived at this conclusion - there is little doubt that Sainovic shared this approach and Milosevic's plans. This is a fabrication and it's total nonsense. Paragraph 694, well, the Prosecutor said there was little doubt, there was little doubt, little doubt, that Sainovic knew about this. In other words, he had to know, based on what? This is all somehow ill defined. You know, there was a professor of criminal law when I went to school, perish the thought, this was so long ago. He said that any indicia in the world must stoop before a single piece of evidence. This is all just indicia, but is this likely, is this sort of likely, highly likely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor of criminal law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He said any --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any indicia in the world must stoop before a single piece of evidence. Indicia are worthless. That's what he was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 696 - I'm getting there - 696 talks about crimes from 1998. It tells us that Sainovic knows about these. If there were any crimes, why aren't they in the indictment? How come the Prosecutor doesn't know? How come Sainovic knows and the Prosecutor doesn't? How does Sainovic get to learn about this? Where does this information come from? I fail to understand. This should probably be drawn from paragraph 698 where he says that he attended meetings, but nothing was said at these meetings about who was perpetrating the crimes and how. What is discussed there is some operations. Well, it's a long road one has to take from operations to crimes. Paragraph 707, as evidence of the efficiency of Sainovic's methods for collecting information, the Prosecutor is taking an event here which has been taken out of the indictment. Somebody introduced himself as Sainovic and spoke to Djordjevic. Whether it really was Sainovic and what he spoke about is something nobody knows; however, that is sufficient for the Prosecutor to conclude that the topic of conversation must have been Racak, and these are the basis for his arguments. Paragraph 708, the Prosecutor says that Sainovic must have known that Drewienkiewicz said to Loncar, but this again is speculation, it's guess-work. The Prosecutor says that Sainovic must have known about Drewienkiewicz's press release of the 1st of April, 1999, but that again is speculation. Paragraph 711, in paragraph 711, everything that the Prosecutor states does not constitute information on crimes. Nowhere in Vasiljevic's statement, P2600, paragraph 62, does it say that Pavkovic informed Sainovic about Izbica. It simply doesn't state that there. Sainovic was providing information about some sort of commission. Paragraph 712, in connection with the crimes mentioned on the 17th of May, 1999, the only thing Sainovic could have heard is that these cases were brought before the courts. There was nothing else that was mentioned. They were dealt with. The mention of crimes, if he learned about them only then, what sort of culpability is that? Paragraph 722, the Prosecutor again says for the umpteenth time that Vasiljevic was the source for the statement that Sainovic was the chief of the Joint Command, that he was authorised to authorise the use of units. All this is taken from a sentence formulated by Vasiljevic at the trial which leaves doubt. It leaves room for doubt, and this is the source for all the conclusions reached about Sainovic and the Joint Command at the time of the war. There's also mention of Dimitrijevic, but the Prosecutor avoids saying what Dimitrijevic testified to before the Court and under oath, and takes its statements from ambiguous, unclear, vague sentences from the collegium of the chiefs of the General Staff and other documents. Paragraph 718 to 724, with the exception of paragraph 722 have no sources. These are all conclusions reached by the Prosecutor. In paragraph 724, the Prosecutor writes about Sainovic's omission, about his failure to punish the perpetrators. Could this be corrected, not 718 to 824, but 718 to 724, with the exception of 722. Paragraph 724, the Prosecutor says that Sainovic omitted to punish the perpetrators, but nowhere can one see on the basis of what authority Sainovic was able to do that as Deputy Prime Minister of the federal cabinet. So I have now finished dealing with all these paragraphs, and all that remains is for me to read my conclusion. I believe that the arguments we have put forward as Sainovic's Defence represent our standpoint, that Sainovic was one of the five deputy federal prime ministers whose position was different from that of all the other accused. He was neither a soldier nor a policeman nor a prime minister or the president of the republic or the state. The Defence has shown that Sainovic performed the same functions in Bulatovic's government as he did of the previous government, that of Kontic. Let's remember that he was at Rambouillet [as interpreted], and that he worked on implementation. Bulatovic formed his government in 1998, and after that the situation in Kosovo began to get more complex. It wasn't Rambouillet, it was Dayton. Before entering Bulatovic's government, Sainovic, as I said, worked on the implementation of the Dayton Accords. That's what I was referring to. Sainovic performed the same function in Bulatovic's government that he had in Kontic's government, the previous one, but the problem of Kosovo grew more complex and grew greater after Bulatovic took office. On the other hand, I wish to show and I hope that I've succeeded in this that only parts of evidence or documents have been presented to you and that these have been interpreted by others and not their authors, especially as regards the Joint Command where Sainovic is nowhere mentioned either as a member or as a leader in 1999. Simply, the Chamber has not heard this. And what is presented by the Prosecution is a combination of various indicia and all indicia have to fall in the face of evidence. Numerous witnesses and documents that the Defence has pointed to do not confirm that Sainovic had the role that is presented by the Prosecutor. If we have to find a solution about the Joint Command, the simplest way to explain the Joint Command, to use a simple analogy such as the one of the drunk driver, let's take Djakovic 's and Dimitrijevic's testimonies and then you can reach your judgement. That's the truth. On the one hand, you have the word of the Prosecutor not supported by evidence but only by indicia, manipulation, and misquotations; and, on the other hand, I believe you have valid evidence brought before the Court presented here before this Trial Chamber. Otherwise, what have we been doing for the past two years? If these witnesses are not telling the truth and if we have to ignore all this, what are we left with? Nothing. For all these reasons, bearing in mind the high level of this Tribunal and everything that I said about this Tribunal, I ask that this Tribunal reach its judgement based on the evidence heard here and then there will be no problems for Sainovic regarding his fate. I propose that he be acquitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. One thing for sure you can rely on is our decision will be based on the evidence we've heard here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't doubt that, not for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now we'll move to the submissions and closing arguments on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you, Your Honours. And I appreciate your indulgence in allowing me to use this stool which for what I hope is just a temporary physical condition. I know it bears a close resemblance to a bar stool, so I hope I don't feel too comfortable or act too comfortable while I'm in it. It's been an honour and a pleasure to appear before this Trial Chamber, and I know that Mr. Visnjic joins me in that, as does General Ojdanic, and we thank the Trial Chamber for the very fair way that you've conducted this trial and for the obviously very close attention you've paid to the evidence over these past two years. I'd like to begin by remarks with a statement made at this trial by Judge Bonomy in March of this year some 20 months after the trial had begun. Judge Bonomy was discussing whether or not the interview of General Perisic should be admitted into evidence. Judge Bonomy said as follows at that time, and this was on 20 March 2008. He said, and I quote: "None of this Bench has read this interview. In one sense, it came to our notice by accident, but that led us to, through curiosity, to at least explore whether it had anything to do with Kosovo since we knew that Perisic was indicted in relation to other matters. So we haven't read it and that's part of the agony for us." Judge Bonomy said "that was part of the agony for us," and so I assume he spoke for the entire Trial Panel. And at least to me and my colleague, Mr. Visnjic, that indicated to us that the use of this rather strong word, "agony," underline the fact that this Trial Panel was here to do justice and was struggling with the question of the admissibility of the Perisic interview because you wanted to know all the facts. And I would also like to think that this passion to know the facts, this "agony," as Judge Bonomy put it, also indicated that after some 20 months of trial, the Trial Panel was still struggling at that time with the question of whether the Prosecution had produced sufficient evidence of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. And it is now our strong submission that after two years of trial, no evidence of guilt beyond reasonable doubt has been presented against General Ojdanic. General Ojdanic is here because on May 24th, 1999, while the bombs were still falling on Belgrade and Kosovo, the ICTY Prosecutor, Louise Arbour, decided to indict some of the top officials of the FRY, political, and military leadership, including General Ojdanic. We can only surmise that this discussion by Ms. Arbour while the war was still ongoing was based on the proposition that because the alleged expulsion of many thousands of Kosovo Albanians was widespread all across Kosovo, it must have been the result of a plan, a joint criminal enterprise. In fact, there was no evidence that General Ojdanic bore criminal responsibility when he was initially indicted in May 1999, and there is no evidence of it now, some nine years later. And it is our submission that the Prosecution has gotten it very badly wrong in this case from day one of the indictment to the present time. What I would like to do now is examine the evidence, first as to General Ojdanic's statements and conduct prior to the war during the period when he was deputy Chief of the General Staff, followed by his appointment as Chief of the General Staff, and, finally, the evidence concerning his conduct during the war. Of course, we'll be discussing this evidence in the light of the well-recognised legal principle that in order for General Ojdanic to be found guilty, the inference to support guilt must be the only reasonable inference available from the evidence. It is our submission that with respect to every major factual allegation in this case, there are inferences to be drawn which are equally, if not more consistent, with General Ojdanic's innocence. I would like to start our decision with what the Prosecution has to say about the appointment of General Ojdanic to replace General Perisic as Chief of Staff -- Chief of the General Staff in November 1998. The Prosecution has claimed throughout in its pre-trial brief, opening statement, and now in its closing brief and argument, and particularly its closing brief, that General Ojdanic and other appointees at that time were seen as individuals who were willing to follow the course intended by Mr. Milosevic in terms of solving the -- in the spring of 1999 the Kosovo problem, the Kosovo problem being ethnic imbalance. This claim by the OTP is grossly unfair to General Ojdanic as a man, as a soldier, and as chief of the army's General Staff. The testimony from a number of witnesses at this trial - and I'm not going to repeat it here; it's set forth in our brief - but this testimony makes it abundantly clear that General Ojdanic from his very early days in the army and throughout the war harboured no prejudice against ethnic Albanians, let alone that he was part of a joint criminal enterprise to change the ethnic balance in Kosovo. Prior to being appointed as Chief of the General Staff in November 1998, General Ojdanic was the deputy Chief of Staff, second in command, and next in line to be Chief of Staff. Moreover, General Ojdanic was not close to Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic specifically stated that he was "less well acquainted with General Ojdanic" when he was being considered for the position as Chief of Staff to replace General Perisic. Mr. Milosevic's comments are contained in the minutes of the Supreme Defence Council of November 24th, 1998, and that reference is to Exhibit P1576 at page 4. Rather than a decision of Mr. Milosevic based on the personal contacts, his personal contacts or knowledge of General Ojdanic, these minutes make it clear that the decision to appoint him was solely because of his qualifications, as these minutes stated, and I quote: "General Ojdanic, when he was the commander of the 1st Army, conducted an anonymous poll among the officers subordinate to him. This questionnaire had 36 items and the results showed that his results with his subordinates were very high in many elements. He holds a masters degree in military science. This is an extremely honourable and good general." Much has been made by the Prosecution in this case, throughout this case, and particularly in its closing brief, that somehow General Ojdanic was a so-called hard-liner, as opposed to the more restrained conduct and policies of his predecessor, General Perisic, another OTP misconception that finds no support in the evidence. Let's look at the record on this. And as we look at the record I'm reminded, Judge Chowhan, of a comment you made over a year ago on May 4th, 2007, to Mr. Hannis, and you said at that time: "Mr. Hannis, I have a question, a little digression from all the seriousness in this. And while arguing, you pointed out, you mentioned about the professional army's role against rogue soldiers. And I immediately was reminded of "Arms and the Man," by Bernard Shaw, and that also pertains to the Balkans. Is there any relevance when he calls those he met chocolate creamed soldiers, any relevance to that?" Mr. Hannis said, "I'm not sure, Your Honour." Judge Chowhan said, "Okay. Thank you." Mr. Hannis said, "Thank you." Well, I probably would have given pretty much the same answer as Mr. Hannis did at that time. I read "Arms and the Man" many years ago, but I went back to it after you mentioned it, Judge Chowhan, and I think there is one theme in this play by George Bernard Shaw that resonates deeply in this case. The play takes place in Bulgaria in 1885 during a war between Bulgarians and Serbs. A Swiss professional soldier, Captain Bluntschli, had been fighting on the Serb side and is fleeing from the Bulgarians. This officer carries chocolate in the pockets of his uniform instead of bullets and pistols. And a light opera called "The Chocolate Soldier" was later based on the events in Shaw's play. So why do I mention this? I mention it because, as we will show, the conduct of General Ojdanic far from being the hard-liner portrayed by the Prosecution was precisely the opposite. The trial record in this case repeatedly shows that when confronted with the choice between war and peace, between bellicosity and compromise, between bravado and restraint, General Ojdanic invariably chose the alternative that would lead to peaceful resolution and not further conflict. There are numerous examples of this. I won't repeat the many collegium references cited in our closing brief beginning as early as 26 September 1997 when General Ojdanic was the deputy Chief of the General Staff. General Ojdanic at that time and throughout his tenure as Chief of the General Staff repeatedly emphasized the futility of the war option and the necessity to look for political and diplomatic solutions. As General Ojdanic said in the collegium of 4 May 1998, as just one of many examples: "The shortest and fastest way to lose Kosovo is by war." And I think it appropriate here to mention General Ojdanic's comments to his colleagues when he first took over as Chief of the General Staff on 27 November 1998. And he said at that time, and I quote: "To what extent I am a hard-liner, how blind or loyal I am, my position on resolving the problems in Kosovo and Metohija, I hope that you know and are witnesses of my participations in the meetings of the collegium if nothing else. Rest assured that in your colleague who has been given the difficult task of leading you, you have a man above all who thinks with his own head and who is his own man. This is how I've been and I remain so, and I have no intention to nor can I change at this very late stage of my career." And I think that this independence of mind is no better revealed than by General Ojdanic's comments to the collegium on 15 December 1997, 3D1076, when he said, and I quote: "During my most recent trip to Kosovo, I met a large number of Serbs in whose heads only the war option is present non-stop, and fools like these can lead us into a war, but I will not stand behind them." As this Trial Chamber knows, there's considerable macho posturing during periods of tension and conflict, and it would have been relatively easy for General Ojdanic to just avoid commenting on the war-mongering of what he then called these Serbian fools. He made these comments before his colleagues on the General Staff, and I think that comments such as these may well have been on his mind when some 11 months later he became Chief of the General Staff and reminded his colleagues that they knew the kind of man he was from their prior collegiums together. This same spirit of both independence of thought and working for peaceful resolution to problems was also demonstrated by General Ojdanic on how he proposed to deal with the members of the Kosovo Verification Mission, the KVM, following the October 1998 agreements. Again, I won't repeat the abundance of evidence cited in our closing brief, but two brief citations to the collegium are illustrative. In the collegium of 17 December, 1998, General Ojdanic stated, and I quote: "The members of the verifier group all have diplomatic status and that is how they should be approached. There should be no forms of crudeness shown to them. This is the least painless form of intrusion, and we should not give them a reason to withdraw," 3D494, page 2. Then one week later on 24 December 1998 General Ojdanic said to the collegium with respect to the KVM: "All commanding levels should study the Security Council resolutions and agreements and demand that they be strictly observed. Nobody in the army has the right to violate these agreements. Adventurism or false patriotism which results in wilful behaviour which goes against the resolutions or agreements must be severely sanctioned because such behaviour could have fatal consequences for both this country and its people," P924, page 27. And I believe it most appropriate at this point to refer the Trial Chamber to the testimony of Canadian General Michael Maisonneuve. The Trial Chamber will recall that General Maisonneuve was a high-ranking member of the KVM in Prizren, and at one point briefly became the operational head of the KVM in the absence of General DZ. General Maisonneuve testified about a memorandum prepared in late December 1998 by a British officer named David Wilson. David Wilson worked for Maisonneuve as an intelligence officer. He was characterized by General Maisonneuve as an astute person who had good knowledge of what was happening on the ground. And if the Trial Chamber would bear with me I think it important to quote the following colloquy from my cross-examination of General Maisonneuve: "Q. And my last question for you, General, is that memo that the same David Wilson, who I think you consider a fairly astute guy, prepared. It's attached to your statement and I ask you about it only because in your statement you said you think it's an accurate assessment of the Kosovo situation." And General Maisonneuve's answer was: "Generally accurate, generally accurate." I went on: "Q. I have hesitate to use it because it is one man's opinion and, you know, he could be right, he could be wrong. But I'm going to ask you about one small part, and this gets back to the simple soldier," and you recall I was asking General Maisonneuve to give us the soldier's point of view, "gets back to the simple soldier if I might I say. And here's what he says. Talking about the VJ, he says quote - this is from the British officer's report - quote: "The key group obviously are the professional officers," talking about once again the army, the VJ, and the SNCOs, the non-commissioned officers, and General Maisonneuve says "senior non-commissioned officers." My question: "Right." Then continuing with the report of David Wilson: "From their point of view, they are frustrated, contemptuous of the the political manoeuvrings, angered at the double humiliation of being scrutinised, the word "scrutinised" is in quotes, "scrutinised by foreign observers in their own land and being required to observe a cease-fire against terrorists, and skeptical, skeptical about the prospects of a policy settlement. While the analogies with Western forces can easily be overdone, it is comparatively easy for any soldier to understand their emotions." "Q. Now, David Wilson was a soldier, was he not? "A. He was. "Q. And, obviously, sir, you're a very high-ranking and distinguished soldier. Do you think there's truth in what he has to say? "A. Absolutely. I think it accurately reflects the feelings from Colonel Delic on down, to probably soldiers on the ground -- of soldiers on the ground of the VJ sources." Transcript 11127-128. And I venture to say that General Ojdanic at the least must have had the same understanding of the emotions of the VJ officers and NCOs, and that, in our view, is what makes even more admirable his insistence on what he regarded as his clear duty to fully cooperate with the KVM, lest cooperation might lead to NATO bombing and war. This even though he also knew that his policy of strict cooperation with the KVM might well be resented by not an insignificant portion of his officers and senior non-commissioned officers. This same pattern and preference of General Ojdanic for compromise and conciliation with the KVM, instead of confrontation, was shown in a number of other ways. The Trial Chamber will recall that General Ojdanic, while still the deputy Chief of Staff, urged that, following the KVM agreements in October 1998, all of the VJ combat groups should be withdrawn to barracks, thus arguing for even more of a restriction than the three company-sized units allowed in the field by the agreement. You can see the collegium of 23 October 1998, 3D645, at page 4. The Trial Chamber will also recall that General Ojdanic arranged for daily rather than weekly reports to the KVM. He also continued to increase the number of VJ personnel assigned for cooperation with the KVM mission, including an increase in the number of English-speaking officers. Having said all this about General Ojdanic's obvious good faith in dealing with the KVM and despite what we regard as an almost fanatical devotion to cooperation with the KVM, the OTP makes a series of misleading claims on this issue as set forth in paragraphs 776 to 782 of its brief. Just about all the OTP's contentions have been addressed in our brief at paragraphs 170 to 185 on General Ojdanic's cooperation with the KVM and paragraphs 64 to 83 on the specific subject of Podujevo as it relates to the KVM. One matter not addressed in our brief to which I now turn is the claim made by the OTP in paragraph 780 that allowing the MUP to keep heavy weapons was a breach of the agreement. This was also mentioned by Mr. Hannis in his oral argument. I note first that this matter actually dealt with the Vienna arms control agreement and not the October Agreements. There's still an obligation to comply. I'm just making a distinction, though, between the Vienna arms control versus the October agreements. And in the collegium of 3 December 1998, General Obradovic had made the suggestion that the heavy equipment could be listed as being with the VJ or as being temporarily with the MUP. There was no suggestion that the equipment should be concealed. The OTP citation of General Ojdanic's comment that he was "not for either one or the other" is out of context. Just before his comment, General Ojdanic actually stated as follows: "Put this problem on paper with brief information and proposal. With regard to these two issues, I will first try with the minister, and after that I must seek the FRY president's position," 3D557, page 20. And, indeed, immediately after General Ojdanic's comment, General Grahovac stated that it was not General Ojdanic but the state who was a signatory to the agreement who would ultimately decide the issue. For the OTP to say in paragraph 780 of its brief that General Ojdanic "was clearly unconcerned" about a breach of the agreement is just not so. We also note the testimony on this point of General Obradovic at TR14977-78 who testified that following this collegium of 3 December 1998, full information was provided by the VJ in compliance with Article 4 of the Vienna Agreement. Finally, on the question of cooperation with the KVM, the OTP in paragraph 777 takes note of General Ojdanic's initial agreement to KVM inspection of barracks. That agreement, by the way, was not the view of General Perisic who, as General Obradovic testified, opposed the authority of the authority to enter barracks; that's at transcript 15034. The reason that barracks inspection did not take place as stated in the OTP brief at paragraph 777 is that, and I quote now from the OTP brief: "Sainovic firmly rejected the KVM's plans for inspections and he was the only individual authorised to permit inspection." From this, the OTP deduces in its brief that "once again, it is clear that Ojdanic supported a fellow JCE participant, this time Sainovic, in furthering the JCE." So we have now reached the point, according to the OTP, that a general is supposed to contest the decision of a civilian authority on a legitimate matter of interpretation; and if not, then the general is supporting a joint criminal enterprise. Ridiculous in the extreme, I respectfully suggest. I wanted to pause here to discuss the significance of the pre-war evidence, including cooperation with the KVM, that we've been talking about as it bears on General Ojdanic's intent. It is, after all, part of the Prosecution's theory that at least as early as October 1998, the joint criminal enterprise to expel Kosovar Albanians came into being. That being so, the OTP presumably would point to alleged non-cooperation with the KVM as evidence that the VJ and General Ojdanic were violating their international obligations and that this state of mind carried over to the war period. I think it might help our analysis here if we briefly refer to the trial testimony of General Dimitrijevic concerning the KVM. General Dimitrijevic said as follows at 26733-34: "My knowledge from this period is as follows: I remember some of the details even today that 90 per cent of the verification mission were active-duty officers of the armies that took part in the setting up of the mission, except that they were not in uniform and they all came from intelligence structures from the intelligence community; that is to say, we had quite a few cases when we realized that members of the verification mission were actually transferring weapons and providing information about the Army of Yugoslavia." So, really, they sided with the Albanian terrorists. At the same time, they asked and in many cases they actually overstepped, they went beyond their mandate, and they asked for information that they were not authorised to ask about. And along these same lines of General Dimitrijevic's mistrust of the KVM, the Trial Chamber will recall the report of British army officer David Wilson as just cited in the testimony of General Maisonneuve, that VJ officers were "angered by the double humiliation of being scrutinised by foreign observers in their own land and being required to observe cease-fire with terrorists who were not even a party to the agreement," which has some relevance, I think, Judge Nosworthy, to comments you made the other day. As I hope we've shown, General Ojdanic strongly resisted this built-in opposition to the KVM even from some of his close associates with full realization and appreciation for the potential of bombing and war that eventually occurred, but I ask this question: What if General Ojdanic had not been as cooperative with the KVM as he was? Does mistrust of the KVM, as clearly expressed by General Dimitrijevic and even relative non-cooperation with the KVM because of this mistrust, necessarily equate with an intent to change the ethnic balance in Kosovo by forcibly expelling Kosovar Albanians? I think that to ask this question is to answer it. And as we go along, I think that this is one of the relevant questions to ask with respect to the resolution of each of the factual sets of issues that are before us. For example, the OTP claims that because he sent troops to Kosovo and March of 1999, General Ojdanic facilitated the joint criminal enterprise. But the build-up of troops, in our submission, has another even more reasonable explanation; that is, preparing to defend against both KLA and potential NATO attack. And as we've already noted, the inference to support guilt must be the only reasonable inference available from the evidence. I'd like to turn now to another instance of the pre-war conduct of General Ojdanic, and that is the proposition that it was General Perisic who presumably against the wishes of Mr. Milosevic was in favour of the limited use of the army and that absent a declaration of a state of emergency, the army should not be used to conduct anti-terrorist operations. As we pointed out in our brief, this is not the time for a parliamentary debate on this subject; but at the least, the constitution and army rules of service make it clear, as I believe Professor Markovic testified, that there was ample basis to support the conclusion that the use of the army was justified in carrying out anti-terrorist operations without the need to declare a state of emergency. Now, where did General Ojdanic stand on this question? Contrary to the claim of the OTP, the fact is that General Ojdanic shared General Perisic's view of the limited use of the army and, indeed, was equally if not more restrictive than General Perisic on this issue. Let me first illustrate this point with some documentary evidence that has not yet been discussed in the briefs. I refer the Trial Chamber to the collegium of 26 October 1997 when General Ojdanic was the deputy Chief of Staff at a time when there are meetings and demonstrations by groups in what were deemed radical antigovernment actions. Here's what General Ojdanic said at the time: "During demonstrations, limit the use of military motor vehicles to a necessary minimum; prohibit the use of vehicles at night except when the brigade commander judges it necessary. In this period, cancel all planned activities which require large-scale movements and the engagement of VJ forces. In addition to what I have said, I believe that the order should strictly prohibit any actions and conduct of VJ commands and units exceeding the constitutional role and tasks of the VJ and which would irritate our public and the international public in particular," 3D1074, page 23, an early recognition of not irritating the international public because he knew what trouble that could eventually and did, indeed, lead to. Now, immediately that comment by General Ojdanic, here's what General Perisic had to say: "All right. Anybody else? Do you have anything to say regarding the organizational groups under your command? There are contradictory opinions regarding the viewpoint that the VJ should not irritate, just as Ojdanic has said, and there are opinions that the army should directly demonstrate for us; that is to say, plan and carry out activity in Kosovo with the aim of discouraging by demonstrating force." Now, as General Perisic said, there were contradictory opinions to General Ojdanic about the use of force. So this is an early example in October 1997 of General Ojdanic's continuing policy of restraint in the face of provocation, just as he denounced Serbian war-mongering fools, as he put it, at a collegium a few months later in December 1997 and as he did a year later in December 1998 when he was the army Chief of Staff and strictly prohibited adventurism in false patriotism by any members of his staff in dealing with the KVM. There are a number of other examples of General Ojdanic's policy of limiting the use of the army while he was the deputy Chief of Staff. At the collegium of 10 April 1998, General Ojdanic said: "As far as our engagement in the curbing of the armed rebellion according to the plans at our disposal we have, they must be carried out after the decision has been made by the competent organs," 3D657, page 2. This echoed the policy of General Perisic. In the collegium of 10 July 1998 when he was the deputy Chief of Staff General Ojdanic: "As concerns certain views according to which we should extend the scope of the army's engagement on certain tasks, I do not agree with that, General. In particular, when this concerns the protection of the population, we should not embark on that position. We have the Serbian MUP forces for that," 3D641, page 2. Later on in that same collegium pages 2 and 3, General Dimitrijevic stated: "When it comes to protection of the population in over 200 villages, that part is going on in an organized fashion." General Ojdanic had a response to that comment of General Dimitrijevic, showing an even more restrained view of the use of the VJ. General Ojdanic said: "I do not know what Aco," that's General Dimitrijevic, "I do not know what Aco means by the protection of the population. It is completely natural to assume that if we positioned a certain number of units deep within Kosovo and Metohija, that their purpose is predominantly to provide psychological support to the population and I think that the direct use of units is a very sensitive issue." In his military expert report, General Radunovic concluded from this college of 10 July 1998 that: "General Ojdanic opposes this direct use of the VJ for the defence of civil population and settlements, for that would surely lead to a general war in Kosovo and Metohija," 3D1116, paragraph 25, page 78. I'm happy to go on, Your Honour, but this might be an appropriate time for a break. I think we're fairly close.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sepenuk. We shall adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00, when your submissions will continue.
